subtopic: APPROVAL OF PROTOCOL ON ACCESSION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, January 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the protocol to the North Atlantic treaty on the accession of the Federal Republic of Germany, signed by Canada at Paris on October 23, 1954, and that this house do approve the same.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF PROTOCOL ON ACCESSION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, so far in this debate we have been listening to the experts. We have had experts speak on the political, military, security and defence phases of rearming Germany. We have listened to one hon. member tell us why he is opposed to rearmament. I think that at least on one thing we are unanimous in this house, and that is, this is one of the most difficult problems we have had to face. Certainly, it is the most difficult problem we have had to face since I came into the House of Commons. I am sure that is true for everyone in this house.
Having listened to the experts, I want to say something about the more human aspects of this problem and what I believe is going on in the minds and hearts of the Canadian people. It seems strange indeed that we should be asked to deliver arms on a silver platter to a people who were our bitter enemies ten short years ago. I believe that instinctively most of us would like to vote in the negative because our memories are not that short. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has explained why he is voting against the rearmament of Germany. We all listened *carefully and I do not think we ever doubted his sincerity. But, Mr. Speaker, he left us with the scales unbalanced. He highlighted the dangers of the rearmament of Germany, but he did not highlight the dangers of the alternatives.

What are the alternatives? During the past month I have received scores of letters asking me to vote against the rearmament of Germany. I have seen almost as many delegations. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I can say that I have not refused to see any person or persons who had opinions on this subject. Even when I knew they were communist-inspired delegations or letters, I saw them and I read them. It seemed to me this was no time for one's personal prejudices. Many of those who came to see me were not communists, but loyal, patriotic and worried Canadians. On this same subject of rearming Germany one hon. member in the British House of Commons said foreign affairs is a choice of difficulties. No truer words were ever spoken. Our choice is a Russia armed to the hilt on one side and on our side an unarmed vacuum in the middle of our own defences.
When I have asked the people who came to see me and to ask me to vote in the negative what the alternative would be, they have said, negotiate and keep on negotiating. They have said, better 1,000 years of negotiating than one day of war. As the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) said yesterday, the allied foreign ministers have already held 352 meetings with Russia over the Austrian peace treaty. We are no nearer settlement than we were 352 meetings ago. I say, by all means let us keep on negotiating, but not through fear. Let us negotiate in equality.
In arming Germany we are not, as I see it, obliterating our chances of negotiating. In fact, I believe we are actually broadening the avenue towards peace. There are no more realistic people in the world today than the Russian leaders. They know, as we know, that it is better to bargain and negotiate through strength than through weakness. I believe nothing proved this more conclusively than the Berlin airlift. When the Russians blockaded our lines to Berlin the ingenuity and imagination of men was enlisted to overcome the blockade. Brains, not guns, were used. There was no war. As soon as the Russians realized that they were beaten at their own game, they capitulated.
No, Mr. Speaker, I have come to appreciate that you cannot bargain or negotiate in weakness. But it does seem to me that the government has been woefully remiss in explaining to the Canadian people why Germany should be rearmed. In foreign affairs, this government seems to adopt a very patronizing attitude, a sort of papa knows bekt attitude; a children should be seen but not heard attitude. Perhaps that was all right when our voice did not amount to much in
North Atlantic Treaty
foreign affairs, but today it does count and no one man or group of men should take it upon themselves to make these decisions without consulting parliament.
An articulate politician in the United States in the person of Mr. Adlai Stevenson once wrote:
Unless the great political parties and their spokesmen assume responsibility for educating and guiding the people with constant candor, how can we be sure that majority rule will meet the test of these searching times.
I feel that this government has not assumed any responsibility for educating and guiding the people on this very complex problem.
There has been much talk in the house about an unarmed Germany being a dangerous vacuum in Europe. Yesterday the minister said that we of the democracies abhor vacuums while the Russians step into them. That is exactly what has happened in Canada between October and January. The government allowed a vacuum of ignorance to emerge. The communists filled that vacuum with the fears and natural apprehensions of the Canadian people. For one thing, the fellow travellers of communism have been playing hard on the fact Germany will be in the atom bomb race. Until yesterday the government did nothing to explain exactly where the atom bomb came into this picture. Until yesterday the government did nothing to reassure Canadians as to the safeguards that are being devised. Until yesterday the government did nothing about the elaborate system of arms control that the allied powers planned.
Is it any wonder the Canadian people are confused, apprehensive-yes, and fearful of what this parliament is doing. Those Canadians who look with favour upon the communist line have been quick to seize upon a Gallup poll which was taken on November 24, 1954. Their interpretation of this poll is that 61-6 per cent of the Canadian people oppose a new German army. That is not the true picture, Mr. Speaker. I believe it is the fault of the government and not of the people or of the poll that it is not a true picture.
I believe that any one of us, if we had been asked such questions without any background knowledge, with no explanation, no ramifications, would have said no, too. The government has made no effort, despite the millions spent on publicity and public relations bureaux, to inform the people. The first question in this particular poll was, can you tell me what the initials EDC stand for? Only one in five Canadians knew the answer. There were 74 per cent who could

North Atlantic Treaty
not answer at all. The next question was, if Germany were allowed to have her own army, do you think it would be a step towards peace or away from peace? There were 43 per cent who said it would be a step away from peace and 27 per cent said towards peace. There were 26 per cent who had no opinion whatever.
In summing up, the Gallup poll itself has this to say:
If it had been practical to include the fine shadings of the control question, results might have been different.
I question the word "practical". I do not think anyone knew the fine shadings of the control question in order to ask it, and certainly they did not know the answers. So there is a vacuum that this government has allowed to emerge between October and January.
Mr. Speaker, I am going to vote for the inclusion of Germany in NATO-not because I like it but because, after a great deal of honest study and much soul-searching, I believe it is the only alternative. I believe it is the safest step for peace. I believe it is the practical rather than the sentimental step toward a sane and civilized world.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF PROTOCOL ON ACCESSION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been presented with what is apparently, on the face of it, an innocuous resolution, and we have to give a decision on it. But I suggest that this innocuous resolution is more like a package deal than anything else-and I am supremely suspicious of package deals. Because while this resolution deals only with the admission of Germany to NATO, there is not one member in the house who does not realize that what lies behind it, unsaid and unwritten, is the rearmament of Germany. And there is not a member in the house who has yet spoken, either for or against the motion, who has not expressed his fear of it.
We have been told that we are faced with a calculated risk, and that is true. Most of our policies in external affairs must be calculated risks. But a calculated risk can be either a success or an uncalculated disaster. There is not one of us who does not hope that the net result of this agreement will mean success, for the sake of the peoples of the world; but there are many of us who fear that, unhappily, the outcome may be uncalculated disaster.
This is not the first package deal we have had in parliament. We had one some years ago when NATO was presented. I supported NATO then for reasons which at the time I considered adequate and which, in retrospect,

I still consider adequate. To some substantial extent the western world had disarmed after the war. But we saw what happened in Czechoslovakia; we saw what happened to Poland; we saw the encroachment of international communism, and for our own sakes it was essential that a line be drawn. But in diplomacy you can only draw a line when you have guns behind it, and that line is only as strong as the calibre of the guns.
And so I supported rearmament because it was put before us-and rightly so at that time-as something which was urgent, imperative and for our own well-being. But there was also something else in that package deal; and I supported NATO as much for article 2 as I did for the rearming of this group of allies.
Article 2 is the article which promised us some hope of economic and political co-operation on the Atlantic. I remember my friend, who was then the hon. member for Vancouver East and is now the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis), saying back in 1947 that there was going to be no safety for the world in an arms race, or in military alliances, but that the solution had to be achieved in another area, which was the area of economic co-operation. Apparently the government of the day believed that. They went to Washington, and Canada achieved some prestige throughout the world because of this article 2, which was presented by Canada and which is known as the Canadian article.
Yesterday, dealing with aspects of NATO other than military, the minister said that NATO is potentially more than a military alliance. I thought so, too, Mr. Speaker. But how potential is "potential"? When are we going to get some results? When are we going to get some action?
The minister said that we are seeking to develop a North Atlantic community. I would like to see a North Atlantic community; but what practical proposal is this government going to make to develop that sort of community? I may be told, "Oh, we are making private protestations". I am not remotely interested in private protestations. I want public declarations of policy so that I know where the government stands in respect of its own child, article 2 of NATO.
We said-and I believe there are many who agreed with me

that if NATO was going to be strong defensively it had to be strong economically. We have iterated and reiterated this at -wearisome length throughout the years, and our warnings have been valid, even though they have been ignored.

In 1949 the government were all for article 2; they were proud of article 2. But through the intervening years, down to the present, there has been a weary shuffling back on the road from Damascus. There has been nothing done, so far as any significant effort is concerned, to achieve what we want. And one of the troubles today, not only in this House of Commons but in the western world, is that we are facing the problems of 1955 with minds which still dwell in the years before 1939. There has to be a shaking up in our thinking.
Some six or seven years ago the government saw the necessity for economic co-operation, because fear was in the hearts of the people. The government saw the light, but now that light is spluttering to ignoble extinction. It is not good enough.
Article 2, the creature of this government, up to the present has been a lamentable failure, and the government must take the responsibility for it. For we were in a position to give leadership. It is not too late to give that leadership, but if we fail to do so the failure will be a suicidal failure.
I have been told that there is no alternative to the calculated risk set before us. I do not believe it; I simply do not believe it. There is one, but we have never tried it out -for what reason, heaven knows. Whether we lack determination or vision I do not know; but I do know we have not tried out the alternative.
Yesterday the minister said there are certain courses which we can pursue. He said that we could keep Germany disarmed and neutralized. That is a policy which I exclude immediately. I do not say it is not possible, but I say it would be unutterably stupid to pursue such a policy, because the net result could only be that the Germans would be left so embittered and vengeful that war would be inevitable.
The minister said that, as a policy, we could do nothing, and hope that something would turn up. I repudiate that policy for reasons I have given before, the chief reason being that it is impracticable.
The minister suggested as another policy that we could give Germany back her sovereignty, without any conditions attached. I reject that, because it solves no problem and would not solve the problem before us in this house today.
Now we have been presented with another solution which the government itself accepts. We have been invited to vote to bring a rearmed, sovereign Germany into NATO.
North Atlantic Treaty
This is an invitation I decline, for the basic policy which the government has been pursuing in the last few years is wrong.
There is another policy, that of putting the horse before the cart. If I may digress for a moment, hon. members in this house realize as well as I do that throughout this country the concept of the Colombo plan has received acclaim, and is popular throughout the nation.
On the other hand, NATO is regarded with apathy. On the Colombo plan we are going to spend this year the niggardly miserly sum of $26 million, but because the people know that this is something positive and affirmative and something which will help the world, they are prepared to go for it in an infinitely greater measure than the government apparently believes; yet on NATO, if we include capital expenditures, we may spend $1,000 million this year. There is nothing but apathy and, in some areas, dislike. Who is to say that the instinct and the judgment of the Canadian people are wrong because they feel with justification that NATO is nothing more than a military alliance? NATO is something vastly different from that which we envisaged and that is why we feel that our hopes have been betrayed. There is a lesson to be learned from this.
But let me ask this question. Why must we always restrict our calculated risks to the area of defence? This is the only field in which we have done it up to the present. Is it not possible that, for the sake of all concerned, we should take a calculated risk in the field of economics? We have agreed that it is essential to our security that our allies be economically strong because only if they are economically strong can our defence be strong. That follows, I suggest, as day follows night, and yet there has been so pitifully little done by this government to make our allies as economically strong as I should like to see them, and therefore there is a possibility that our defence will be correspondingly weakened.
Obviously the more prosperous nations are the more they are able to share their prosperity with those who are less fortunate, and the more secure we all shall be. Prosperity is indivisible. But a lead has been given, of which this government is aware, by a most distinguished American who, in his wisdom, saw what ought to be done. He who is now the President of the United States said a few years ago, as commander in chief of NATO, that before we embark on German rearmament the first

North Atlantic Treaty
thing we must try to achieve is the economic and political integration of Germany with the rest of Europe. That is the course we should be pursuing, but the government has put the cart before the horse. Arms must come first. I say that policy is wrong. I say that economic co-operation with political integration must come before we do the other, if we desire security.
If article 2 has the validity which I, with faint hopes, still think it has, it is the duty and responsibility of this government to lead, to take a calculated risk in the field of economics, and I offer a suggestion. I today am speaking for myself and none other. What I say commits nobody and no other; but I offer this suggestion. If we are serious in this business of economic co-operation, we should suggest to our allies that, on a reciprocal basis over the next ten years, we are prepared to reduce our tariffs and barriers to trade 10 per cent a year. And I argue that, as a result of the enlarged markets which would ensue, all of us would be much better off than we had ever dreamed possible. Prosperity would become more of a reality than certainly it is now.
There is a risk. Certainly there is a risk, but it is a risk which would capture and hold the imagination not only of our people but of all those who are our allies and friends in Europe. It is an offer which would win acclaim, perhaps as great as Churchill's, when in the darkest days of the war he made that offer to France of which this house knows. There are those of you who may say that this suggestion is fantastically impossible. Mr. Speaker, there was nothing more impossible than that a member of this parliament should have risen in his place in this house a decade ago and said that we were going to rearm Germany within ten years. That was the impossibility of impossibilities, but it has happened. I question very much the validity of impossibility in politics anyway. As for it being fantastic, is there anything more fantastic than the threat of destruction by thermonuclear energy?
There is nothing impossible about the suggestion if we mean business. We pursue that course and we give hope to millions, we give leadership to those who are desperately seeking leadership. Unfortunately we have not yet been able to break away from the bonds of our own national sovereignties.
The government apparently prefers the calculated risk of rearming Germany before insisting on the economic and political integration of which I spoke. It may be said {Mr. Stewart (Winnipeg North).]
that I am arguing for a European community. I am not, because I do not think a European community in itself is viable. I am arguing that we must work with Europe. Whether we like it or not, we are ineluctably bound up with Europe, so we ought to realize what the future may have in store for us.
Let me ask another question. Why is there this speed in rearming Germany? We have been told on all hands by those who are in a position to know that the international situation is such, that tension has so decreased, that we can perhaps feel a little more secure than has been the case during the last few years. Yet we intend to rearm Germany.
Now, I have no illusions about Soviet policy. We have to safeguard ourselves against the effects of Soviet policy, but I assume the same calculations are in the minds of those who say that the situation today is somewhat less tense than has been the case for some years. But why the hurry? Why the need for another 12 divisions when there are proposals before the United States congress now that there be a reduction in American forces between 300,000 and 700,000 men. Is it the idea that those 12 divisions will take the place of those Americans who will now return to their homes? Why this hurry, if other NATO nations feel that the international situation has sufficiently improved for them to reduce their own commitments? Why then the addition of another 12 divisions in Germany?
I have no means of knowing that this is so, but I read newspapers like other hon. members and I have read speculations on what happened in the last NATO meeting, where apparently those who in responsible positions suggested that the goal set in Lisbon two or three years ago was too high; that we do not need today the same level of conventional arms; and that therefore perhaps we could lower that level. If that is so, why do we ask Germany to rearm itself with conventional arms and throw another 12 divisions into the military kitty? The answer may be-this again is supposition-that the NATO staff may have decided if there is going to be another war atomic weapons will be used but merely in a tactical sense. I hope that is not true. I cannot believe it, because if they are used in a tactical sense, they are going to be used in a strategic sense. Once atomic weapons are used, thermonuclear weapons will be used, and the fields of the earth will be white with the ashes of humanity.
One can always argue, of course, that if there is going to be a war we have nothing

to worry about, for if thermonuclear weapons are to be used we shall not be here to do any worrying. Why the hurry then to have these 12 German divisions, if the situation is obviously better than it has been for some years?
The answer is American pressure. In 1950 the American chiefs of staff decided that Germany was going to be rearmed. In the fall of 1950 the NATO ministers agreed that such would be the case; and because of this, and the pusillanimity among the western allies in refusing to stand up to the United States, we now have this problem before us. Let me quote from a journal which I am certain must be the bible of all Liberals the world over, the Manchester Guardian, in its issue of September 23, which had this to say:
About EDC Americans really ought to realize that it was an expedient hastily devised because the United States blackmailed its European allies in 1950.
That is why we are faced with this problem today. There is no military need for this haste, but there is imperative need for haste in the field of economic and political co-operation and that is the one area in which we have seen none. It may be argued that Europe has failed. That could be so, but I suggest that whether it has failed or not the government owes it to its own people to try once again to make economic cooperation a reality.
We are being asked to rearm Germany. We cannot be blamed if our minds sometimes dwell on history. We cannot be blamed if we have doubts that history has perhaps outlived itself. I am not one of those who would suggest for a moment that the German people are inherently warlike. I do not believe that they are. I know far too many people of German descent in this country to believe that, and I know the active part they have taken in democratic organizations. Yet if I may translate what I have to say into simple musical terms, there is the Germany of Beethoven but there is also the Germany of Wagner.
I know that there are thousands of German refugees from Hitler who have returned to their own country in an attempt to recreate and rebuild it on a democratic basis. I know that in my own city there are Jewish people who are alive today because of the valour of individual Germans and groups of Germans in helping them to escape. I know that there are tens of thousands of Germans who are buried today in Germany who were victims of Hitler's concentration camps. To suggest for a moment that you
North Atlantic Treaty
can indict a nation is extraordinary nonsense. And yet we have these questions. We know that Jews and Ukrainians and Poles in their millions were murdered by German troops. Today it may be so that the relatives and friends and countrymen of these dead, in their magnanimity, are prepared to forgive for the sake of world peace; but they are never going to forget.
I am not going to mention the revulsion which all of us felt and still feel when we remember the concentration camps of Germany, because revulsion is not a substitute for policy, and abhorrence is not an alternative to policy. But these things cannot be forgotten.
There are certain facts which we must bear in mind. There is the fact that in the past the nationalists and militarists came to power and led their people, and those people followed them except for a valiant minority. There is the probability that Germans were politically immature. That can be argued against. It can be said that here is the fallacy of post hoc ergo propter hoc and that such a situation does not exist today. I can only hope that such is the case, but I have no proof.
There is the undeniable fact that today in Germany nazis are in key positions in government and business. To suggest for one moment that nazis will not again get into the army is arrant rubbish. We have been told that there are millions of young Germans who oppose rearmament. Are they likely to be the ones who will enter this new army of this new reich? No. Those who are going to enter the army will be the spawn of former nazis. To suggest that the screening will be sufficiently effective to keep out the nazis is nothing but wishful thinking.
I state as a fact that the reception given Kurt Meyer was not an accident, that it is indicative of a state of mind which is perilous to all of us, even although there were many Germans who deplored it. I state as a fact that what Frau Schlitter said in London was not an accident, that she meant it.
I state as a fact that the Russian face of Germany is a reality. I agree with what my leader said yesterday about what is happening in connection with a German aircraft firm and certain interests in Spain. We can also say as a fact that there is now a Spanish face to Germany. Some German corporations in their attempt to evade the obligations of their country are doing now what they did with Russia in the 1920's.

North Atlantic Treaty
I aver that this will be a fact, that within the predictable future the Germans will want and will get atomic reactors. I affirm as a fact that within the predictable future the Germans will want an increase in their forces and may conceivably get it. I state also as a fact that there are unscrupulous groups in Germany who will go to any lengths in an attempt to unite East Germany with the west. Then what will we do? We are told that there are safeguards, that those safeguards are in the treaty. What if the United States decide that they are going to support this war against communism and communist barbarism in eastern Europe? What then do we do? What control do we have as a matter of fact over what the United States may do, despite this talk of the Atlantic community. There is no community and this government must take its share of responsibility for that fact.
There is no one in this house who wants Germany rearmed. The only ones in Canada I can think of who want the Germans rearmed are the communists of Canada, and for obvious reasons. They know that the only country which can offer anything to Germany is the Soviet union. Russia can offer Germany a reunited country, and local communists may be looking to the day when a rearmed Germany will be joined with the Soviet union to try to dominate the world in so far as they can.
All of us have been subjected to communist pressure in the last few weeks. It is nothing new. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis) said the other day, there is no group in Canada which has more gall. It is those same communists who in 1939 were prepared to fight Hitlerism, who a few days later were prepared to lick the boots of Hitler's nazis, and who now again because of Russian policy are prepared to pursue the course dictated by the Kremlin.
There are some who are quite in favour of German rearmament. One has only to read the business pages of the newspapers to realize how United States steel interests are looking forward with some anticipation to German rearmament. We know that there are industrialists in the United Kingdom who feel the ferocity of German competition in the markets of the world and who want to see Germany rearmed in the hope that it will curb their power to compete. Then there are those who welcome German rearmament, those who have been so aptly termed in the past as merchants of death. Yet surely the greatest fact before the house is that there are millions of Germans today, knowing their own country as they do, knowing their own countrymen as they do, who are opposed to its being rearmed, and we are thrusting arms upon them.

There is another aspect to this calculated risk. There is an element of gamble in it and the gamble is the possibility of an old man living another two or three years, the gamble that Herr Adenauer will survive the next two or three years. I would hope that he does, but what is the alternative? Suppose he does not; what sort of government do we get then? No one knows; no one can speak with certainty. But that is far too big an X in this equation to be glossed over lightly.
I do not deny the need for generosity to a beaten opponent. Germany must be brought back within the comity of nations and as rapidly as possible, though not on Russian terms. There are some who feel that further discussion with Russia would be futile; some who feel that further discussion might be useful; some who feel, as I do, that the suggestion offered by Premier Mendes-France is worthy of consideration, namely that meetings should be held with the Soviet union in May.
But surely again the obvious fact is that if Russia was afraid of Western German rearmament she would have reached an agreement long ago. I do not believe for a moment that the Russians have any great fear about the rearmament of Western Germany. But this much I am certain of, namely that Germany will be united when Russia is ready to give them union, and not one moment before. Not all our blandishments or speeches will alter that situation.
One of the unhappy facts we must face is that when we meet the Russians we never speak the same language. We use the same words but when the Russians say "democracy" they mean tyranny; when they say "justice" they mean iniquity; and when they say "life" they mean death. That is a fact we will have to remember.
I am one of those who feel that perhaps another discussion with the Soviet union on Germany might be fruitless. Nevertheless, it is imperative that there be discussions as soon as possible with the Soviet union on other and wider matters. The time is not far off when we shall have reached what somebody called "the intolerable atomic absolute," when certain people in the United States feel that Russia has got the air power and thermonuclear power necessary in one blitz to extinguish the west. What do we do then? What happens when some trigger-happy fool shoots? It will be the death of all of us. It is imperative that we meet the Russians and we continue to meet them until we can arrive at some modus vivendi and modus operandi. But this is an interpolation.
I come back to my charge that the government has not followed the path of economic

co-operation as I am convinced it should have done, and the government is wrong in saying there is no alternative. Of course, it may be said that no matter what I say, no matter what my feelings are, and no matter what my colleagues say, Germany is going to be rearmed in any event. I believe that to be the case.
If this agreement is not approved in other countries, I am convinced that the nationalists in Germany will rearm bilaterally with the help of Washington, and if not with Washington then with Moscow. No matter what I think or do, I for one am faced with a fait accompli. I am faced with the choice of an armed Germany with controls or an armed Germany without controls, and I must accept the controls no matter how ineffective ahd inadequate I may consider them to be.
But to refer to myself again, what do I want? There can be only one answer, to my mind. I want these controls in existence if Germany must be rearmed, because I think it is essential for the welfare of all of us that they be there.
We all know what happened with EDC but I still believe we have got to go forward with this concept of integration. I did not agree with the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) yesterday when he paid tribute to the United Kingdom for departing from its age-old policy of not putting troops into Europe. I believe the EDC met with failure in the French assembly in large measure because of earlier British refusal to co-operate in Europe.
Too late the British again have divisions in Europe, and here, Mr. Speaker, is the supreme irony, namely that France agrees to German rearmament if the United Kingdom keeps a number of divisions in Europe to protect France against the consequences of that German rearmament. How illogical can we get? Yet I as an individual and as a member of the Canadian parliament am faced with this package deal. I am faced with a deal wherein German rearmament, which I oppose at this time, is tied in with the necessary controls on that rearmament. I am faced with the accomplished fact. I support the controls. I oppose this resolution for what is not in it, and I support it for what is in it.
Someone yesterday mentioned Scylla and Charybdis. I refuse to be devoured by one or engulfed by the other. Some perhaps may show their feelings in this matter by being absent from the house when the vote is called. I shall not be absent. I shall be in my place in the house and as a matter of deliberate policy I shall refrain from voting.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question which we are debating today is of major importance for the western powers which, for the past ten years, have had to withstand the constant aggression of communist countries.
For the past ten years, the western powers have sought the most appropriate steps to take in order to convince Russia and her satellites to abandon their ideas of aggression.
The experience of the past few years has established without doubt that the Soviet will keep on talking of peace while threatening the world with war as long as the nations on this side of the iron curtain continue to show disunity and weakness.
That is precisely the fact which we must not lose sight of during the present debate.
The problem we are facing, as an anticommunist country, is the mustering among the western nations of the strength required to deter the communist powers from pushing forward on the road to aggression to an ultimate world conflict.
The rearmament of Germany within the framework of the western European union and its admission into the North Atlantic Treaty Organization are only means to an ultimate end: the safeguarding of world peace and the pursuit of happiness for the whole human race.
It is only natural that well-disposed people here and elsewhere do not see without some concern Germany becoming overnight a free and sovereign nation, and even an ally. It is a surprise for a great many people to learn that we are committing ourselves to defend, in case of attack, this very Germany which brought so much hardship and suffering to the world, and which has been guilty of heinous crimes against entire peoples.
Such a feeling of apprehension towards Germany should be easily understood, and we must, indeed, respect it. However, I think that the agitation that for the last few weeks has been coming from a small group of communist traitors here in Canada only shows how much confusion was thrown into the ranks of the Russians and of their varletry throughout the world by the stand taken in Paris by the western nations.
It is no doubt difficult to forgive Hitlerite Germany for all the misery she spread over the world from 1939 to 1945 and we will long harbour inevitable resentment on that score. But we must be realistic. It would be well to remember the words spoken by George Washington in his farewell message to con-

North Atlantic Treaty
gress in 1796. He spoke words which, to this day, remain topical, with regard to the foreign policy of his country:
Nothing is more essential than that permanent, inveterate antipathies against particular nations and passionate attachments for others should be excluded . . . The nation which indulges toward another a habitual hatred or a habitual fondness is in some degree a slave . . .
That is why I believe we must rejoice at the result of the London conference and the signature of the Paris agreements. On the eve of these historic conferences, the countries of the west were just emerging from a terrible impasse into which they had been thrown by the rejection of EDC by the French national assembly. It spelled disaster for the west, especially for American diplomacy in Europe.
Germany was again a vacuum in the very heart of Europe and we, who were preventing her from rearming, were in the obligation of defending her, in spite of herself, if she were attacked. The only alternative left was to abandon her to the Russians or to leave her in neutrality, which amounted to the same thing.
The unification of the peoples of western Europe appeared as a very distant possibility and the Soviets were already beginning to rejoice at our division. Those were indeed dark days for the governments of the free countries of the world.
Fortunately for the free world, France had at that moment the dynamic leader she had been awaiting for ten years, Mr. Mendes-France. He was able to regain the confidence of his country's allies, at a time when France was beginning to discredit herself. Thanks to him, she was able to assume her responsibilities.
England, which by keeping out of EDC would have made that pact non-viable, did not fail either to take her responsibilities. By undertaking to maintain forces in Europe for 44 years, England was able to take part in these negotiations, to direct them and to bring them to a successful conclusion. With England out of EDC, France would have been alone to bear all the odious part of the rearming of Germany. France would have been alone to face its secular enemy. The stand taken by England saved the day.
We must be practical and I think that the London and Paris conferences are happy dates in the lives of free peoples the world over.
The western European union gives back to Germany its full sovereignty and permits her to rearm, but we must not forget that that extension of the Brussels treaty of 1948 is a defensive pact and that there are in the new protocol some very sound guarantees against any intention which Germany might have of turning against its new allies.

Lastly, its admission into NATO, which, as I have said, is another defensive pact, guarantees to the countries on this side of the iron curtain an army of 500,000 men which we cannot do without. There again, NATO control of Germany's armed forces is an excellent guarantee of German intentions.
May I quote two statements that are expressive of the advantage this German rearmament may mean to the cause of peace and of the free nations.
This is what the assistant supreme commander of NATO forces, Marshal Montgomery, had to say after the Paris agreements:
The integration of German forces into the Atlantic forces will, once these troops are trained, constitute a solid rampart against an eventual menace of aggression by the Soviets.
The Paris agreements are decidedly more satisfactory than the former EDC, insofar as they leave much greater freedom of action to the allied military commander.
General Gruenther was equally categorical. He stated:
If an organization like this had reached the same efficiency in 1939, I am inclined to think that the second world war would not have taken place. We now have to perform the great task of putting the new agreements into effect. Above all we need the full support of public opinion. I am convinced we will get its support because the 400 million people protected by NATO realize that our essential aim is to prevent a new war and the destruction of our civilization.
The spirit of sincere co-operation and of trust which is so evident since the Paris conference inspires me to believe without reservation that in two or three years we will have solidly consolidated peace in Europe.
Such declarations, particularly that of General Gruenther, enable us to understand the military importance of these new agreements. I believe that every sincere Canadian will greet those agreements as a great step towards the establishment of a common purpose among our free countries in the face of the aggressive and destructive totalitarianism of the Soviet world.
There is only one way to live in peace with the Russians, and it is to show them unequivocally that their designs of world domination will never succeed.
I hope that all the members of this house will vote in favour of these agreements in order to indicate clearly that the people of Canada loathe communism, and rejoice at the evergrowing unity among the free peoples of the world.
I would like now to discuss another aspect of this question, and I must admit that there arises in my mind some doubt and apprehension.
We are called upon today to vote the admission of Western Germany into the Atlantic nations organization, of which Can-

ada is a member. I am convinced that it will be carried with the unanimous consent of the house, but I believe that this vote affords us an opportunity to review the situation, and to ask ourselves whether our government, in the international field, is not being carried away and compelling our country to play a part which is beyond its strength and means. I rather feel as if the government has an exaggerated tendency to play the part of a world power.
No doubt this country enjoys a fine reputation throughout the world. It does have very real importance in world affairs, but it must not be forgotten either that we only have 15 million people.
Canada too, whose people have a real craving for peace, must not, moreover, give the world the impression that it is a venturesome nation willing to take a hand in all wars, whenever and wherever they occur. The history of the last few years gives an opposite impression. We have unfortunately taken part in the last two world wars, and in the Korean war; we have troops within a few miles of the iron curtain; we have an armistice commission in Indo-China. In brief, we are everywhere in the world.
That is why I believe it to be important that, in this debate, the government explain clearly to us the new obligations involved in the Paris agreements and the part Canada will be called upon to play in the future by reason of these agreements.

The position of our forces in Germany was never too clearly defined, for at the end of the war, when the time came to occupy Germany, we were simply thrown out. But today we are back there, we maintain a brigade of 10,000 men a few miles from the iron curtain, and we maintain an air division in France.
But, as regards our troops in Germany, we were the only country which has had to pay its expenses. The United States, England and France had full divisions there but they were occupying powers and as such the care of their troops was borne by Germany.
North Atlantic Treaty
It is a good thing for Canada of course nbt to have a reputation for stinginess, for shirking her responsibilities, but why should our country do more than others and especially more than a nation of 15 million people can afford?
When the war in Korea broke out, our country's effort was far above that of most countries in the western world.
It may be that our friendship with the United States justified such an effort. But we can ask ourselves if, compared to all the countries of the western world, such an effort was really suited to our international status.
I sincerely believe that the government shows too much enthusiasm for international ventures and that it always wants to play a prominent part. It may be that it has very good reasons for doing so, but it could give us a lot more explanations than it has given us so far.
The other night, on a C.B.C. forum, one of the most distinguished members of the press gallery, speaking on that very subject, used a phrase which gives us, I think, a very good idea of the situation. He said;
Are we getting too big for our breeches?
That is why I say that if Canada, as a member country of NATO, had to be represented at the Paris agreements on October 23 by its Secretary of State for External Affairs, some may ask why the minister had to go to the London conference. Rumours were circulated in the press to the effect that he was not even invited and had to insist in order to be able to attend.
We have, no doubt, some interests to safeguard in Europe. But if the west European representatives were in London to discuss German rearmament, they were meeting as the delegates of EDC nations. Having signed the Brussels treaty, England was considerably interested in the matter, and the United States, as leader of the western nations in the cold war, also had to attend.
But Canada had no more business to be there than Greece, for instance, which is also a member of NATO. And yet, Greece, which had much greater reason to take part than Canada, was, during the last war, invaded from both sides at once, by Italy and Germany. That country was not represented there. It is still a victim of Hitler's Germany. Moreover, on one of its frontiers it touches the iron curtain. Still, it was of the opinion that the question could be decided without its intervention. The same thing applies to the other members of NATO who, as was the case for Canada, did not have to sign the western European union agreement.

North Atlantic Treaty
It may be that these great European countries, whose diplomatic traditions go back several centuries, could not make any decision without the advice and the knowledge of our minister. That may be but one may doubt it.

It is possible to doubt. We have the right to ask ourselves whether we were then furthering the interests of our country or whether once more the government was not carried away by its megalomania.
Or whether our government, in order to gain an international prestige out of proportion with our means, does not run the risk of leading us into ventures likely to be detrimental to the economy of this country.
First of all, we must be realistic, and weigh carefully the means and needs of this country, before embarking upon too big ventures which might be very costly.
The colonial policy followed for the last ten years by England and France gives us a perfect example of that realistic view.
Realistic England, at the end of the war in 1945, granted complete independence to India and Pakistan. These peoples, following this action by England joined the commonwealth voluntarily, signed trade agreements and pledged themselves to safeguard British interests in those countries.
Great Britain had proved to be realistic and this realism had been to her advantage. But France, more sentimental, who likes repeating the sonorous phrase "France's mission in the world!", refused to act likewise in Indo-China so as not to lose any prestige. She was therefore forced to wage an impossible war in this colony, a war which deprived it of the best part of its young officer corps and shook the economy of France to its foundations for a period of eight years. Mendes-France's realism was necessary to end this conflict.
I feel that this little example should be considered by our government since, in foreign policy, especially, idealism must be replaced by realism. Here, as elsewhere, prudence is the mother of virtue. That is why I believe that the study of the Paris agreements provides our country with an opportunity of weighing its responsibilities with proper realism and of asking ourselves if our foreign policy is not such as to lead us into certain ventures beyond our strength, our obligations and our needs.

The reasons for supporting this resolution introduced by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) were fully stated by our leader, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). We have given serious consideration to this problem, and in view of all the circumstances have come to the conclusion that we have no alternative.

I might say that I have had only five communications in respect to this matter; two of them from my constituency, one from Toronto, one from Vancouver and one from Ottawa. But in speaking to my constituents I have found that, without reservation, they believe there is no alternative to ratification of this agreement.
The reports coming out of the U.S.S.R. give us hope that Russian imperialism may have a difficult time in keeping its own people under subjugation. If time plays in our favour, then the decay and deterioration of the Russian dictatorship will be the largest single factor in establishing a lasting peace. Let us sincerely hope that time will be on our side.
Now, Mr. Speaker, many hon. members have expressed regret that parliament was not called to discuss this very important matter. At the conclusion of this debate, I should like the government to state clearly why the members of parliament were not called together to discuss this problem in order that they might make suggestions and give guidance in drawing up such an agreement. This would put an end to the speculation we have heard throughout the country. We have all heard speculation as to why we were not called together. Some say it was because of the by-elections; some say because of the Quebec tax situation; and others say it was because of the pressure of members of parliament. In conclusion, therefore, I request that the government state clearly and fully why parliament was not called and taken into the government's confidence.

speechtext:
It is with a large measure of hesitation, Mr. Speaker, that I ask for the floor on this occasion. The subject matter under discussion is probably as important as any with which this house

will ever be called upon to deal. It relates not only to the security of Canada, which should have top priority at any time in our deliberations, but it relates also to the security of humanity itself. I am sure that since 1947 all of us have followed with deep concern the apparent unwillingness of the Soviet union to be satisfied with living her own life within her own borders in peaceful co-existence with the rest of the world. Slowly but surely we have reluctantly found it necessary to refashion our weapons and reconstitute our armed forces.
I can recall when Sir Winston Churchill came to this continent back in 1946 and made a very famous speech at Fulton, Missouri. I can recall the feelings occasioned by the Berlin airlift. I can recall listening to the radio when President Truman declared the state of emergency in 1947. I remember during the 1949 election, when I first came to this house, NATO was the word that was on everyone's lips. At that time our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said that the North Atlantic Treaty Organization would be the foundation of our foreign policy and our security. Later on I remember very well EDC and I am sure those words are recalled here very earnestly. All these events were steps leading slowly but surely to the erection of a defensive shield by the NATO nations of the western world. The erection of that shield was provoked only by the communist threat exemplified by Kremlin-directed action wherever on the globe defensive forces were not strong enough to discourage their forward movement.
Canada as a young country has been proud of the fact that the NATO shield was the outgrowth of an idea that had its birth in the mind of our own Prime Minister. And we are also proud of the fact that our own ministers, notably the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), the former minister of finance and the former minister of national defence had a great share in building the NATO alliance, and played a prominent part in the development of that NATO idea.
I recall here in Ottawa less than a year ago the supreme commander of the NATO forces, General Gruenther, addressing most of us in the railway committee room. He pointed out a gap in the centre of that NATO shield which was to be filled by German divisions in EDC, and everyone at that time accepted that as a matter of course.
I think I should mention here that many well-meaning Canadians, many of whom served in the last two wars, have expressed concern over the rearming of Germany. We
North Atlantic Treaty
can only look at the over-all security picture, and make our decisions on the facts as we find them at any particular moment in time. We are not gifted with second sight, and we cannot look into the future.
The honest doubters could prove to be right. And in that connection I want to read one sentence-although taken out of context, it expresses very clearly the point I have in mind-spoken by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). He said:
On the one hand we of the democratic world dare not be naive. It would be foolish and dishonest to pretend that those who are most sceptical may not be right.
That is taken out of context, and it does not apply to this particular subject. I do suggest however that the words are applicable.
On military matters we must accept the advice of the country's military advisers. That advice together with the advice of our allies in two world wars has brought us victory and made it possible for us to reach this point in time. This country has good military advisers. We have not the manpower available that is found in Asia. Our military advisers have said that from the point of view of manpower we require integrated in our western defence the divisions that can only be supplied by West Germany. They advise-and this has been done publicly in the newspapers; it is not new-that without a rearmed West Germany, together with our weapons, our shield is not sufficiently strong to defeat a thrust from the east. That advice was given before the latest hydrogen bomb development.
The risk in not rearming West Germany is too great, and not arming West Germany would not be keeping faith with those Canadians who have died in the first two wars.
Having in mind that picture, I remember last summer the feeling of dismay I experienced when I read in the newspapers about the rejection of EDC by France. And I remember with what feelings of suppressed alarm I, as a citizen, watched from a distance while our Secretary of State for External Affairs, Great Britain's Sir Anthony Eden, Mr. Mendes-France, Mr. Adenauer and Mr. Dulles resolved their different viewpoints and hurriedly but surely evolved the solution which was to fill that gap in our NATO shield that we are ratifying today.
The things being decided here today are fateful for humanity, and it would be unthinkable for Canada to refuse ratification when France, perhaps the one country that has suffered most in our memory from an aggressive Germany, after so much heart-searching finally found within herself the strength to

North Atlantic Treaty
rise above her fears and to agree to this important instrument. Let us hope their uncertainties are in the past.
However, this afternoon my purpose in speaking goes beyond this point. During the period of the events which I have outlined there has been a rapid change and growth in the power of atomic weapons, and I think there should be a clear distinction between atomic warfare and weapons and hydrogen or thermonuclear warfare and weapons.
I note in this agreement that hydrogen weapons are classed as atomic weapons, and rightly so, but the destructive power of hydrogen devices is so far beyond the power of what were first called atomic bombs that they should not be confused with one another. It is very important that the distinction be clearly understood.
The term "atomic weapons" should be confined to fission devices in which the nuclear power is produced by the splitting of the atom, as opposed to fusion devices, notably hydrogen or thermonuclear devices, whereby atomic power is released by a fusion of atoms brought about in the heat of the ordinary atomic bomb, which is used as a trigger. These devices are not limited as to size, as are conventional atomic weapons.
With this distinction, atomic weapons can and should be classed as conventional weapons because, terrible as they are, they are only larger concentrations of power of weapons already known and used. Thermonuclear weapons on the other hand are so far beyond this that they carry within themselves the possibility of the suicide of humanity- and I want to make that point with as much force as I ca .
To support this statement I would quote only a few Lines from a speech by the Minister of National Health and Welfare when he spoke in New York last October on the question of disarmament. These are his words:
There are reasons to believe that progress under present circumstances may be less difficult than it has been hitherto. For one thing, I think it quite possible that men in the governments principally concerned on either side of the iron curtain are beginning to fear the awful power that scientists are putting at our disposal. Certainly I am not ashamed to admit I myself find the situation most disquieting. For the stakes are incomparably higher than they were even a few years ago. I think that only those associated with governments which have some direct experience of atomic processes and direct access to classified information of technicians working in this field can be aware how serious is the threat which contamination and other effects of nuclear explosions can pose to the very existence of organic life on this planet.
None of us should be ashamed, or too proud to admit that we are concerned. Humility before the awesome power which our scientists are placing in our hands is, I suggest, a becoming attitude for members of governments in any part of the world.

I want to make a very important point in connection with this protocol, in the light of what I have just read. If we show weakness anywhere, our only possible enemy has shown that he will take advantage of that weakness.
If we do not plug the hole in our NATO shield by ratifying this protocol and bringing into the western camp the necessary manpower represented by the West German divisions, we leave ourselves unprotected against the military advance of communism in the vital centre when considering only the field of manpower together with conventional atomic weapons. Communist manpower is many times greater than ours, and the only restraining factor would then be as now the hydrogen bomb which ought never to be used, but which we will surely have to use if we fail to meet our responsibilities. Man as an individual does not possess the right to take his own life. Humanity similarly should not have the right to take action that is tantamount to committing suicide. We are therefore morally obligated to do our utmost to maintain an adequate shield of conventional weapons-when I say "conventional weapons" I mean atomic weapons-integrated with available manpower against the threat of communist expansion. If we do not ratify this protocol, we are deliberately failing to meet our responsibilities not only to Canada but to humanity.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) yesterday said something that was very true. He said:
I believe that in this world today we are playing for time. We need it terribly. There are things that we can do if we are given the time. The Secretary of State for External Affairs, as I have already suggested, referred to the tremendous forces being made available to us as science gets down to the power of the atom with its tremendous peacetime uses. If we had the time I think mankind could yet turn this world from one of recurring wars to one of permanent peace and human accord, with a high standard of living for mankind the world over.
I agree wholeheartedly that we must have time, but the only way we can get time is by plugging that hole.
I want to say just what having time means. It is not just something simple. We cannot say we must have a little time to do some more negotiating. I was fortunate a few years ago to work as an engineer in another country, on another continent, where those whom I was supervising, or many of them, were people whose skin was of another colour than mine. I had one lad who was a good smelter man, and I would match him with any of our Canadian boys. His name was Jampie. As in this country, when somebody does a good job and there is another job open that pays a little more money you are

anxious to promote him. Just such a situation came up and 1 said to Jampie, "There is a job open on a converter; would you like to have it?" He looked at me and said, "No, boss, I eat porridge; I don't eat bread." His pay was 4s. 3d. a day. The job he turned down paid 5s. a day. He had thought it over carefully. The extra 9d. would not give him the necessary bread to make up the extra physical work he would have to do on the other job. When he said "porridge" he meant cornmeal porridge; that was the basis of his food.
You can take all the grain surpluses you like. You can load them on ships. You can drop them in that country out of the goodness of your heart, as many tons of grain as you wish, but that act would not put the extra bread in Jampie's stomach. In this country we have been expanding our economy at the rate of between 3 and 4 per cent a year, and that is faster than human beings have ever done it before. In Jampie's country the rate is roughly the same. It would be unrealistic to expect to expand it faster, but that is the only way you can put the extra bread in Jampie's stomach and in the stomachs of other Jampies.
It is a problem that requires patience. The process of expanding the economies of these undeveloped countries is slow, and they must do it themselves in the long run. It will not be done overnight. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said, their economies will truly and surely expand with our aid, and then the words of the hon. member will be fulfilled; but I should like to put it differently from the words he used in his paragraph. I would say I am confident that we shall have the time, and I am confident that we shall turn this world from one of recurring wars to one of permanent peace and human accord, with a high standard of living for mankind the world over.
I feel that my vote on this occasion will be only one among many that will contribute to that end. If we do ratify this protocol, if we continue to support the ministers in this house who have contributed largely to its present degree of success, then, in "keeping with the motto in the personal seal of Lord Ismay, secretary general of NATO, which was affixed to this protocol, we may "have no fear."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am confident that had anyone in this house in 1945 suggested that by 1955 we should be doing what we are doing today that person would have been considered a very fit patient for a psychiatrist. Nevertheless the question before us is of great significance to every Canadian man, woman and child.
North Atlantic Treaty
In my opinion, nothing that has come before this house since the end of the war has been so important as is the question before us.
Notwithstanding the significance of the matter before us, Mr. Speaker, there is just no enthusiasm among the peoples of the world today for the ratification of this protocol, no enthusiasm except possibly on the part of those remaining members of the German military staff and on the part of those who believe that war with Russia is inevitable.
Could I believe that war with Russia is inevitable then I should certainly be supporting this protocol. War, like politics, makes very strange bedfellows, and certainly if it is inevitable that we are to get into a third world war with Russia, then it does not matter much whom we have for our allies so long as they have an abundance of thermonuclear weapons.
Although the protocol has been ratified by the assemblies of a number of the nations concerned, there has been little enthusiasm for this ratification in those assemblies. There was very little enthusiasm in the British House of Commons, where 51 per cent of the members representing both political parties refrained from voting. There was very little enthusiasm shown in the French assembly, which was induced to reverse its first vote by the threat that France would be isolated and that Germany would be rearmed with or without French aid. There appears to be very little enthusiasm in Germany itself, as is indicated by the report in this morning's press of the delay which is being caused there to the ratification of this protocol.
Certainly there is no enthusiasm across this country. A Gallup poll released by the Canadian Institute of Public Opinion on November 24, 1954, showed that 27 per cent of those who were interviewed thought that the rearming of Germany was a step toward peace, but that 43 per cent of those interviewed thought it was a step away from peace. It is true that one in four of those interviewed in that Gallup poll had no opinion on the subject; and it is true that 74 per cent of those Canadians who were interviewed had no conception of what was symbolized by the letters EDC. That, I suggest, is a reflection on the government, a reflection on the press of Canada, and to some measure a reflection on ourselves as members of parliament for failing to give to the Canadian people information on this subject which is one of vital importance to every Canadian. Certainly, 1 have found no evidence of any enthusiasm in my riding.
I have received, to date, well over one thousand personal appeals asking that I oppose this resolution. Those personal appeals

North Atlantic Treaty have come from individual trade unionists, from individual veterans and from other citizens. Some of these are people in my riding that I know to be communists, but I know the people in my riding well enough to know that hundreds of those protests came from people who are just as violently opposed to communism as any member of this House of Commons.
Why should there be any enthusiasm for this measure? Even the members of this chamber who have spoken in favour of it have shown their misgivings. Few of them have shown any great enthusiasm for the step we are taking here; the best they can do is to hope that they are right.
The objections and the misgivings of that small minority of us in this chamber who will vote against this resolution were very clearly set forth yesterday, in no uncertain terms, by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and they were also expressed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) today.
Our objections were furthermore expressed by the C.C.F. leader yesterday, even though he could not in all conscience agree with us. They have been repeated by many other speakers in this house who are supporting the measure. I shall not take the time of the house to repeat some of our objections which have already been stated. As I have already indicated, I do not believe, I cannot believe in the inevitability of a third world war. I cling to the belief that such a catastrophe for the human race can be avoided, but I cannot believe that the step we are about to take can possibly achieve any purpose other than to make the avoidance of that catastrophe more difficult.
I am concerned with the possibility of the resurgence of German militarism, and I think it is only sensible to realize that by taking this step we are encouraging that resurgence. I just cannot for the life of me see how we can think otherwise. There can be no doubt that those who will control German rearmament will be members of the former German general staff. I do not think there is or can be a doubt in anyone's mind that many of those who were members of the former German general military staff during world war II will now be in charge of that rearmament.
It is only sensible to realize, as has been pointed out, that a rearmed Germany will in a short time become the predominant force among the western European nations. In this connection I should like to read one short paragraph from Lord Russell's new book, "The Scourge of the Swastika." He makes reference to the German general staff, some

of whom we must remember will be in charge of German rearming, and on page 4 he gives the verdict of the international tribunal in connection with the German general staff, as follows:
They have been responsible in large measure for the miseries and suffering that have fallen on millions of men, women, and children. They have been a disgrace to the honourable profession of arms. Without their military guidance the aggressive ambitions of Hitler and his fellow nazis would have been academic and sterile . . . they were a ruthless and military caste . . . Many of these men have made a mockery of the soldier's oath of obedience to military orders. When it suits their defence, they say they had to obey; when confronted with Hitler's brutal crimes which are shown to have been within their general knowledge, they say they disobeyed. The truth is that they actively participated in all these crimes, or sat silent and acquiescent, witnessing the commission of crimes on a scale larger and more shocking than the world has ever had the misfortune to know.
I believe, regardless of our opinion on the necessity of ratifying this protocol, that we must face the fact that a rearmed Germany will again come under the direction of those same military leaders.
If a third world war is inevitable, then the resurgence of German militarism does not much matter. It will make very little difference to any of us what general staff is in the ascendancy under those circumstances. What I am more concerned with than the resurgence of German militarism is the effect this ratification will have upon the process of negotiation with our enemy.
Three years ago we were told how vitally important EDC was. For three years we were taught that the western allies could not survive without the ratification of EDC. But for three years, without the ratification of EDC, we made what is admitted on all sides to be more progress in negotiating with our enemy than at any time since the end of world war II. Why then the haste? Why the hurry? For that period of time we have made real progress on reaching agreement through diplomacy and negotiation without having recourse to arms. Must we now take this step which, if it does anything, will in my opinion make negotiation extremely difficult?

speechtext:
I doubt if the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) has made a single speech in this house within the past year without emphasizing the fact that we have been making progress in the field of negotiation, and no one has been

louder in claiming that we must not close any door to the possibility of reaching agreement through negotiation and diplomacy.
We negotiated on Korea. We have made some progress in negotiations regarding Indochina. We have, thanks to the good work of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), made some progress toward convening another conference on disarmament; and, if we accept press reports, we are now on the point of negotiating a cease-fire on Formosa.
We have been making progress, Mr. Speaker, and to my mind the most important question concerning the ratification of this protocol is the effect it will have on the negotiations in future. Will it hamper or improve our chances of settling disagreements with Russia through negotiation? If I could be as certain as is the Secretary of State for External Affairs that it will open the way to easier negotiation, then I would have no hesitation in voting in favour of ratification. But for the life of me I cannot see how this is going to make it easier for our negotiators to reach agreement on the many international problems confronting us at the present time.
Most of all, I am concerned with the effect the ratification of this protocol will have upon the outcome of that conference which has been initiated through the good work of our delegation at the United Nations under the leadership of the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
All Canada was proud of our achievement at the United Nations. All Canadians rejoiced that our own delegates and one of our own ministers was able to do what the United Nations has been trying to do for many years, namely, get unanimous agreement on the possibility of another meeting on disarmament.
We have the communists with us, Mr. Speaker, and we are going to have to live with them. If we are to avoid a third world war we must, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs told us yesterday, find some way of reaching an agreement on an effective disarmament program. Just so long as east and west continue to pile up armaments of every known nature, just so much greater becomes the danger of someone somewhere sparking a third world war. Unless we want a third world war we must find some way of reaching an agreement on an effective disarmament program.
As I have already indicated, it appeared that we were making some progress. I am most concerned with what effect this will have on our meeting with Russia in a disarmament conference after and not before we have rearmed Germany.

North Atlantic Treaty
One effect of this protocol is certain. Both east and west will acquire more arms. Both east and west will strengthen their military forces. One result is sure, whatever else may be in doubt. We will be adding to our forces in the west, and we have no reason in the world to suspect that Russia on the other hand will not offset any military balance which may be created by the rearming of Germany by further rearming of the forces of the Soviet and her satellites.
There is another question. At the end of world war II I participated in a conference of the Canadian teachers' federation. As educators we were then concerned with the fact that there was in Germany a whole generation of German youth who had absorbed the philosophy of nazism. I well recall the concern of the Canadian teachers' federation and the world federation of teachers over what steps should be taken to try to eradicate from the minds of that generation of German youth some of the things they had learned under Hitler, and how we could possibly educate in Germany a generation of youth who would have some conception of the ideals and philosophy of democracy.
There have been a great many democratic leaders in Germany since then whose chief concern has been to train a generation of German youth with some conception of the ideals of democracy; to get them away, to enable them to forget the lessons they had learned under Hitler. Under this protocol we rearm Germany and we shall place these very youth, with whom democratic leaders have been struggling for the past eight or ten years, under the military leadership of at least some of the men who led the German forces in world war II. That, I think, is a matter which we should consider seriously.
The government, with the support of the majority in the house, will obviously ratify the protocol. I can only hope that history will show I am wrong and those who support the protocol are right. But I must be guided personally by my own conscience, and I can follow no other course than to take issue with the Secretary of State for External Affairs, for whom I have the very highest regard, take issue with my own leader, for whom I also have the very highest regard, vote against the measure, and leave my constituents to be the judge of my actions.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to say anything in this debate. I did not feel that I had any particular competence in the matter now before the house. However, I think the speech made by the
