hon. member who has just taken his seat does justify a modest intervention on my part.
I should like to say first of all, as he has just said, that whatever the differences each of us may have in our various points of view we all respect the points of view of other hon. members on a matter of such great importance, and certainly nothing I shall say is to be taken as a reflection on what the hon. member has said, on what any of his colleagues have said or may say, or in any way a reflection on any other member of the house.
But I do think the hon. member is in error when he suggests that there is no enthusiasm in this country for this particular proposition. I am sure the word "enthusiasm" in this context should be defined. No one, for example, has any enthusiasm for the payment of income taxes, but our people recognize that if we are going to discharge the responsibilities of government at the present time taxes have to be paid, and in that sense there is "enthusiasm" on the part of the Canadian people for this particular obligation. Surely there is enthusiasm on the part of the people of Canada for the maintenance of peace and freedom in the world. Surely those of us who believe that peace and freedom can best be maintained at this time through this particular proposal will find it possible to justify the stand we are taking on this momentous question.
I have said that, within the context of my understanding of the word "enthusiasm", I believe there is a strong conviction, soberly arrived at, if you will, on the part of the people of the country that, having in mind the realities, there is no alternative for those of us who want to preserve what the west stands for other than to take every legitimate opportunity to align ourselves now with that potentially mighty nation that has always played such an important part in the history of Europe and of the world.
There is one group in our country, of course, that does not like this particular resolution, and I am not suggesting in any way that the hon. member or any other hon. member of the house is directly, willingly or unwillingly a party to the points of view of this group. I have noted in the Canadian Tribune that on December 10 the national committee of the labour progressive party met in Toronto at which time, according to this paper, the leader of the labour progressive party, Mr. Tim Buck, issued a call to all L.P.P. members for country-wide action against ratification of the London and Paris

agreements. I learned, furthermore, that a detailed directive was later issued by that party setting out with considerable care the manner in which the campaign against ratification was to be organized. I am sure that all of us in the house have already felt the effects of this particular way of impressing us with the extent to which there is no enthusiasm in the country for the decision that most of us in the house think has to be taken with regard to this matter. I have had placed in my hands through a responsible source a copy of the particular directive to which I have just made reference, and here it is:
Every section of the party should be activized in this campaign. All possible initiative should be developed in neighbourhood activities. Members of parliament should be visited by deputations in their constituencies.
The idea should be raised of a great national delegation to Ottawa at the opening of parliament, if necessary.
That petitions of a local character be taken up by individuals. We should have small, and preferably handwritten petitions organized in such organizations as the Y's, trade unions, shops, and neighbourhoods. Every comrade can write out a short petition and take it to his or her neighbours, getting 10, 15 or 20 signatures and then forward it to their M.P.
No single petition is being issued at this time in order to avoid the difficulty generally encountered of people refusing to sign a petition because it might associate them with the left.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that if there is no enthusiasm on the part of the people of Canada, it could be because this directive has already been acted upon. But we are not unfamiliar with this technique, and none of us in this house is going to be in any way influenced except, as the hon. member who has just spoken has said, by the dictates of his or her own conscience.
I feel that the majority of the people in this country, in the exercise of what their conscience suggests and having in mind the great stakes involved as well as the challenge of the ideology which since the end of the first war has faced the free world, will recognize that, great as are the difficulties and so-called risks involved, it is our duty at this time to let the people of Germany know that the integrity of that nation and the preservation of the freedom of the world rests with the west and not with the east.
It seems to me that is the positive feeling which I, for one, would want the people of that nation to realize at this time. We want them to feel that, notwithstanding the justification of the judgment of history against the atrocities of another regime in that country, we would hope that in this interdependent

world we could march with them in the future toward the building up of a fabric of peace and not of human destruction, to which admittedly they have made their contribution in the past.
A moment ago the hon. member referred to the work of the Canadian delegation at the recent general assembly of the United Nations. What we should do, he said, is to work for disarmament. We should seek to channel the resources of the world, now being deployed into the building up of machines of war for destructive purposes, into channels for constructive purposes for the good of mankind. The hon. member said that should be the purpose of this government's policy and should be the attitude of this parliament and of this nation.
I am sure that upon reflection he would admit that that is the purpose behind the policy of this government, that that is the purpose behind the policy of the governments of the United States and the United Kingdom. I feel it is necessary that we should declare here and now, as the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) did when he spoke in New Delhi, that we do not for one moment subscribe to the view that either our own policies or the policies of our great neighbour have any other purpose than to bring about peace among the nations of the world.
I went to the meeting of the United Nations to assist my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who realized that certain matters would take him to Europe on at least two occasions during the course of the autumn. During the first week of the ninth assembly of the United Nations I was able to confer with him on the purposes that should guide our point of view in respect of the various questions that were to be discussed at the United Nations. Naturally as a member of the government I knew of the difficulties that besieged the North Atlantic community in Europe, and the part that Canada would be expected to take at those important conferences in London and Paris.
My colleague left the United Nations before a speech was made by the permanent delegate of the Soviet union, the late Andrei Vishinsky, on September 30. This was one of the most important speeches made by the late Mr. Vishinsky at the United Nations, for it announced the abandonment of the traditional attitude taken by the Soviet union on disarmament. In effect he said that from now on they would no longer insist first upon an agreement to ban the use of atomic weapons as a condition precedent to disarmament in
North Atlantic Treaty
conventional weapons. That represented a very important declaration. I at once communicated with the Secretary of State for External Affairs and pointed out to him the nature of this declaration by Mr. Vishinsky. He replied that we should immediately take every advantage of this situation, even to the point of taking the initiative to see if we could not take some forward step on this question at the United Nations.
Those who criticize the proposal now before us as one that is contrary to the peaceful purposes to which this country is dedicated ought, therefore, to bear in mind that while my colleague was taking a particular step in London and later in Paris, it was as a result of his instructions, and I might say his inspiration, that we decided to take the initiative at the United Nations to see whether or not the time had arrived when we could count upon the support of the Soviet union to take solid steps toward a program of disarmament.

I do not think there can be any doubt about that. Now, because of the remarks made by the hon. member who took his seat a few minutes ago, I want to recall certain steps that we have taken. To make this particular question more understandable to hon. members, I may remind them that two years ago the United Nations set up a disarmament commission. It surely is the function and responsibility of the United Nations to do what it can to ease the burden of armaments.
Last June my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs had taken steps along with M. Jules Moch of France, Mr. Selwyn Lloyd of the United Kingdom and Mr. Patterson of the United States, in discussions in London, to see whether or not it would be possible to give new life to the cause of disarmament through renewed meetings of the subcommittee of the disarmament commission that had been set up for that purpose. Out of those discussions in June came a notable document known as the Anglo-French memorandum, which provided a formula for disarmament. This formula was subscribed to by the United Kingdom, France, Canada and the United States, but was opposed by the Soviet union, represented at that time by Mr. Jacob Malik.
The speech made by Mr. Vishinsky on September 30, therefore, came as a most heartening bit of news to the world, and

North Atlantic Treaty
particularly to those who had followed these discussions. They argued that even at this seemingly most illogical time we might bring about an easing of the burden of armaments. So we decided in Canada-that is, our Canadian delegation-to put forth a resolution urging the reconvening of the subcommittee that had met in London in order that the discussions that had ended there so abruptly, because of the attitude of the Soviet union, might be resumed. And in view of the speech made by Mr. Vishinsky we thought we were perfectly justified in putting forward this proposal.
As an earnest of our intention we took the unusual step of circulating to the United Kingdom, to France, to the United States and also to the Soviet union an advance copy of the resolution we proposed to introduce the next day, together with a letter addressed to the permanent delegate of each of these countries. I was given the assurance at once by the three countries of the west that we could count fully on their sponsorship of the resolution we intended formally to lay on the table the next day, and Mr. Vishinsky himself called me to say he greatly appreciated this act of courtesy, that his country was anxious to give consideration to the implications of our resolution, and that while he could not say more at that moment, certainly he would look on the matter with the greatest interest and sympathy.

I refer to the three gentlemen who accompanied me in my conversations with Mr. Vishinsky. I can say that whatever credit there may be for what was done should go, in large measure, to them for their advice and their help, as well as their great industry.
But the fact is that after a series of meetings we were able to arrive at an understand-ing_the United States, Great Britain, Canada and France on the one hand, with the Soviet union on the other. I think I may say my impression is that we were able to arrive at an understanding with the Soviet union because by this time the masters of the Kremlin had come to the conclusion that they were negotiating with an area of the world that had become strong.
I am sure the Soviet union respects strength. I am sure we are now in a better position to carry out the proposals for the peaceful use of atomic energy because of our armed strength. I am not saying we will succeed in the matter of disarmament, but certainly we are in a better position to move ahead because of the contribution the western nations have made since 1947 in the building up of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
And so in any consideration of this matter of disarmament, and the part we played at the United Nations, it would be quite wrong for anyone to contrast what we sought to do there with what my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, was able to accomplish in London and Paris. In passing I may say that his speech yesterday certainly did not reveal the very considerable part which he personally played in the successful outcome of the meetings in London and elsewhere during the past few months.
It would be wrong to say that because we were trying to bring about disarmament we were acting in a way that was contrary to what was being done in London, and later in

Paris. The fact is that I really do hope the steps taken by us last fall at the United Nations will mature into successful results. At the last meeting in which he took part at the United Nations Mr. Vishinsky, who acted as chairman of the disarmament committee of the United Nations, formally set in motion the operations of the subcommittee. When the meeting was over-and this was only a few days before his death-I happened to pass him and I said, "I really hope we mean business, all of us, this time."
I do not know whether all of us mean business or not; but I can say this-and I say it to the hon. member for York South- that we did our best at the United Nations to promote disarmament, just as in London my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs did his best, along with others from the west, to bring about guarantees for increased unity among the western powers.
We did nothing that could be construed as an abandonment of the main safeguards which the western powers consider essential for effective control. We made it clear in our discussion that we wanted to argue from a position of strength. If the world before the advent of Hitler had been strong enough, not to resist by aggressive action but by way of defensive measures, it is conceivable that the mad dream of Hitler's war would never have taken place. There was no change in this policy because of our efforts towards disarmament, nor was there any change in the resolution of all of us which would have the effect of weakening the unity of the west. Certainly the United States, Great Britain, France and Canada, who took the leading part in these discussions at the United Nations, did not in any way by that step indicate, or intend to indicate, that we were prepared to abandon the defensive strength that had been built up during the years since the end of the war.
Our policy in Canada, and I am sure the policy of our co-sponsoring western nations, has always been to consider the issue and the time. The Canadian government has always believed that our objective in building up strength for our survival is to attain a position from which successful serious negotiations can begin. As the Prime Minister has said, everything we have done in NATO, at the United Nations or elsewhere has been in an effort to prevent another war.
Now in asking this house to support this resolution we recognize the implications; we recognize the force of the irritations that are recorded in the pages of contemporary history; but at the same time we cannot blind ourselves to the fact that in Germany
North Atlantic Treaty
there is a powerful group of people potentially capable of doing good as well as of doing evil. Whether or not we bring Germany into the North Atlantic community the day will come when that nation will again enjoy its sovereign position, a circumstance which may come about perhaps by action on its own part or by bilateral arrangements made with the strongest power in the west. Therefore what we are now doing is not only to guarantee our own strength vis-a-vis a potential aggressor. At the same time we are giving evidence to the people of Germany itself of our desire to share a peaceful life and a peaceful world with them.
The Canadian government has pursued a seemingly illogical course at London and at Paris, but on examination a course that I am sure commends itself to this house and to the people of this country. By our acts at the United Nations we have demonstrated, along with our colleague nations, that we have no warlike intentions, that we would like to see the resources of our country and of the western world employed for more constructive purposes than the building of instruments for human destruction.
I said on two occasions at the United Nations, once during the disarmament debate and once on Mr. Lodge's proposal for the peaceful uses of atomic energy, that as Minister of National Health and Welfare in Canada I could be expected to have a special appreciation of the moves we were making. I share with every hon. member the hope that the day will come when we will be able to transfer to more humanitarian ends the great resources our people have put at our disposal for the purpose of building up defensive alliances against aggression; that we will be able to use these resources to improve the health and welfare of the people of this country and make additional contributions in these fields to the other peoples of the world. I look forward to that day, and so do the people of Canada. But if that day is not at hand it is not the fault of this nation, it is not the fault of the nations of the west; it is because the policy of the Soviet union, pursued over these years, stands in the way and jeopardizes all that we treasure most. I believe the resolution moved yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) is constructive, is directed toward strengthening our position and thereby making us more respected and a stronger figure at the bargaining table. In a practical way this may do more than anything else to create in our world at this time an era of security, freedom and peace.
