subtopic: APPROVAL OF PROTOCOL ON ACCESSION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are now dealing with a subject that is of critical importance in international affairs. There has been no discussion since the war of greater interest to the Canadian people than this one which deals with Germany. The attention focused on this subject by parliament has been impressive. It is under circumstances such as these that parliament fulfils its great function as a forum in which direction and guidance may be given to the Canadian people. It serves to give opportunity to those who wish to present differing points of view. Here is the place where all the facts may be disclosed, all the evidence examined, and false propaganda exposed and discredited.
It is my intention to support the resolution, for reasons which I shall presently state. If I do not show the great enthusiasm that some seem to think hon. members who support the resolution should show, and have expressed surprise in that regard, on the other hand I doubt whether I shall present very many reservations.
At this stage I should like to commend the minister on his statement yesterday. I think it was well done, though incomplete in some respects. Having commended him, and others have quite properly complimented him-to set the proper balance I should now proceed to offer a little criticism, not in any partisan spirit, for the subject is above party considerations, but because I have been dissatisfied for the last 20 years with the conduct of our external affairs.
My dissatisfaction goes back to the period before the second world war when we faced a crisis in international affairs just as momentous as the present period of uneasy peace. In those years I looked to the government of the day for information and direction, and was sadly disappointed. I have had no reason to change my opinion since that time. The official Canadian attitude to foreign affairs has all too frequently been characterized by
TMr. Martin.]
unwillingness to disclose any information until pressed to do so; to ask for parliamentary approval long after agreements and protocols have been signed; to encourage a so-called bipartisan attitude without prior consultation with the opposition, and to avoid discussion at home and commitments abroad wherever possible.
I remember the late Mr. Gordon Gray don drew attention a few years ago to the small amount of time given by parliament to the discussion of external affairs. Some slight improvement has occurred of late, but more is desirable. Competent as the minister is in his special field, he nevertheless has fallen into error on this occasion due, in my opinion, to long years of conditioning in the bad practices I have mentioned. I shall not blame him for the failure to summon parliament in the fall; that responsibility lies elsewhere. But I do place the blame on him, as did the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken), and on his department for failure to appreciate the necessity of preparing the Canadian people for this measure which is of such historic importance. He has been outmanoeuvred and outwitted by the communists. We are now gathering the fruits of this method of conducting our external affairs.
During the past six weeks members of parliament have been deluged with letters, telegrams and other communications, chiefly but not entirely from communist-inspired groups across this country. The communists have had the best opportunity in years to mislead the Canadian people. Skilful communist propaganda has succeeded in creating in the public mind the opinion that the only issue at stake is the rearming of Germany. Taken completely out of its context and background the rearming of Germany would alarm almost anyone, but considered in relation to the whole sphere of international affairs it is a very small part indeed.
In the four months which have elapsed since the London conference, in the almost three months that have gone by since the signing of this protocol by Canada's representative, no effective information from a government source has gone out to the people of Canada. No official statements or documents were placed in the hands of members of parliament. Even now with parliament assembled the supporting documents have been tabled with diffidence; they have been reproduced in Hansard or in Votes and Proceedings only upon request, and are incomplete. Consider the resolution now before us. It states:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the protocol to the North Atlantic treaty on the accession of the Federal Republic of Germany, signed by Canada at Paris on October 23, 1954, and that this house do approve the same.

In the British House of Commons the motion dealing with the same subject was expressed as follows, and I quote:
That this house approves the policy of Her Majesty's government towards western Europe as expressed in the agreement reached in London on 3rd October 1954 and in Paris on 23rd October, 1954.
I think the motion before us should have included some reference to those conferences. Technically, of course, it is correct. The admittance of Germany to NATO requires the approval of our parliament. Canada is not a member of the western European union, as is Britain. Nevertheless the admittance of Germany to NATO is merely the final step in a whole series, and would not have been considered without the other arrangements between Germany and western European nations. Furthermore, Canada was represented at the London conference and played a full part in the deliberations. Obviously, I think, parliament should have been asked to approve or disapprove of the government's policy as expressed in the agreement reached at London. All we are asked to do is to approve of Germany's admittance to NATO. I give this as an example of the method used for many years past to play down or gloss over matters that concern Canada's international relations.
Then just consider the documents that have been tabled. Instead of putting in our hands a white paper, which would have included the proceedings of the London conference and Paris conference, instead of giving us all that information, what happens? The minister tables what is actually a special supplement to a NATO letter which is undated. This gives practically all the information as to the Paris conference, but omits one very important matter which I shall mention in a moment. Several days later on request a reprint was tabled from the magazine External Affairs purporting to be a report of the final act of the London conference.
On request the protocol was printed in Hansard. Again on request the proceedings of the Paris conference were printed in Votes and Proceedings. The proceedings of the London conference remain simply as a sessional paper. I think following the British custom that documents of such importance, particularly in relation to a matter of this nature, should have been incorporated in a white paper and given to members of parliament as early in the session as possible. I do not understand the operations of the Department of External Affairs in tabling documents of that nature when the other method is available.
Then I say that they are not complete. One of the first questions I wanted answered
North Atlantic Treaty
when I came down here was the actual contribution required of Germany by NATO. What are the figures? People who interviewed me talked about the contribution in rather large figures. I did not know. I did not have the actual authentic information. Nowhere in the documents tabled by the minister is that information to be found. The minister disclosed it yesterday in the course of his speech. In the British white paper dealing with the Paris conference I find a subnote mentioning twelve German divisions, 1,350 aircraft, and naval vessels.
Similarly with regard to the London conference, the documents tabled in this house are not complete because they omit the text of the three statements made by the representative of the United States, the representative of Great Britain and our own minister of external affairs. I think those three statements should have been included in the documents tabled in the House of Commons here.
Having said that, I think the minister can now relax. I trust that he will profit by my suggestions for the improvement of the administration of his department. I would not have taken the time of the house to mention these matters had it not been for the great historic importance of this step that we are considering. We should have all the information that is available to us as members of parliament upon whom rests the responsibility of making decisions, in order that we may answer effectively those who write to us or send us telegrams or come to see us.
I just want to say a word with regard to what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said last night. He was later supported by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), so perhaps the other point of view from that city may be presented. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre expressed the fear that with Germany making a military contribution to NATO and being given the right to rearm, very soon Germany would dominate the councils of NATO. I cannot follow my hon. friend in that reasoning when there are actually 14 nations involved, and when the dominating powers are surely the United States and the United Kingdom.
Then my hon. friend mentioned the necessity of removing the causes of war. I quite agree with the hon. member that the problem of removing the causes of war is of profound importance. That is a problem that has engaged my attention ever since the end of the last world war, and I have given it more attention than anything else. But the hon. member suggested that poverty was one of the prime causes of war. I shall give his

North Atlantic Treaty exact words, so we may be quite clear about them, as reported at page 397 of Hansard for January 20:
Given the time I think we can remove some of the causes of the world's ills. We can change the picture so that instead of two-thirds of the world's people going to bed hungry tonight, as they do every night of their lives, there might be some sharing of the food and good things that we can produce.
I agree with the hon. member that everywhere in this world want should be removed. But I cannot agree that want is a major cause of war, as he implied in his statement. That expression is rather widely used, and people frequently say that if poverty were removed the danger of world war would be lessened. I do not know to what extent it would be lessened, though I agree with the necessity for removing poverty throughout the world.
However, I doubt if any evidence can be produced that any of the great wars of history occurred because people were short of food. It will be a long time before I am convinced that we are in any danger of a third world war because of any action that might be taken by a half-starved peasant in the wilds of Siberia, or a starving population somewhere else in the world. The decision with regard to a third world war or a war on a world scale rests with a few singularly well fed men in the Kremlin.
To digress for a moment, I believe the causes of war should be examined by this house on some occasion. We had a debate two years ago when we touched on that subject, but it should be further examined in order that we may be better informed. I take one of the prime causes of war to be anarchy, that lack of control among the nations of the world which leads to unrest. Each nation is sovereign in its own right and makes its own decision with regard to declaring war on its neighbour.
If we deal with that possibility I believe one of the prime causes of war will be removed. In this regard I believe it is in NATO that the most effective step has been taken to that end. The nations grouped in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization have come closer together than at any time in the history of the world, and gone farther toward solving that problem. They have become so closely integrated that there is not the slightest possibility of any one of those nations declaring war or committing an act of aggression against another member of that group. The hope of the world is that some such system as that can become more widespread. It is in that connection that I look at the problem of Germany. I have not concentrated my attention on the rearmament of Germany. For me


that has been a secondary consideration. It is the problem of bringing Germany into the council of the western nations that impresses me most as it does others who have looked at this picture very closely.
It is a really astonishing step forward to realize that a former enemy-and a bitter enemy at that-is now going to unite with us and sit down at the same council table. When has Germany ever sat down peacefully with the representatives of the western nations with the intention of co-operating with them to maintain peace and security? Not in our lifetime, except perhaps during the short interval of the Weimar republic. Not for 80 years have we had the opportunity of getting close to Germany. Not in fact, since the time of Bismarck. Yet I cannot help but recall that earlier in our history the Germans were well thought of and even admired by some. We have only to recall the battle of Waterloo, when Wellington saw with pleasure and delight the arrival of German troops under Blucher.
I have no reason to like the German people as a result of the experiences I have gone through. I have nothing but scorn for Prussian officers, nazis, and arrogant German militarists. But I do not believe for one moment that all the people of Germany can be put into that category. I believe it is a bit difficult for us to blame anyone in Germany under the age of 30 for any of the atrocities committed during the war.
We have suffered severely at the hands of Germans. Indeed, is there a family in Canada that has not suffered? Nevertheless, has not every family in Germany also suffered? Once you engage in war it is difficult to draw the line between the opposing sides. I make no excuse for the frightful atrocities committed by the nazis in their concentration camps and other places of torture. I make no excuse for the atrocities committed on the battlefield. But in all fairness we must recognize that the German nation too has suffered. That nation has learned a bitter lesson in two world wars.
We have said of France that she would have been a great and powerful nation in our time had she not been bled white during the first world war. We have time and again lamented the loss of the flower of British manhood in the first great war. Is it not therefore likely that Germany for the next 50 years will be lamenting the loss of the flower of German manhood in the second world war? I believe there are perhaps as many widows and orphans in Germany as in any other country in the world.
The suffering therefore has not been solely on one side. We might say that they brought

it upon themselves. But we know that under our own democratic system of government decisions are made to which everyone cannot agree, and we have to go along with those decisions. Decisions were made by German nazi leaders which inflicted serious loss and injury on the entire German people.
For those reasons I am not quite certain there will be the resurgence of German militarism which bothers some people. There may be a reaction against German militarism for a long time to come. But even if there is a resurgence of German militarism I believe the present controls are effective. I do not propose covering those controls again, for they have already been dealt with, and I agree with statements made in this regard by the hon. members for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) and Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes), and the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Well, that is the situation. If we examine history we see that over long periods of years there have been antagonisms between nations, 300 years of it between Britain and France, a very long period between Canada and the United States. It is practically within living memory that the antagonism and fear of Canada of the United States has been dissipated. We are aware of the antagonism between France and Germany ever since 1870. But what is the situation now? Surely this is one of the greatest forward steps in the history of the world. France and Germany, bitter, mortal enemies in so far as we have known their history in recent times, have now agreed to come together. It is something we could not have expected or foreseen.
That is not all. The United States of America, on whom we pinned our hopes during that difficult period in the 1920's and 1930's when the league of nations was formed and then had trouble, has altered its age-old policy with respect to international commitments. One of the reasons I suggested to the minister that Mr. Dulles' speech at the London conference should have been printed in our records was this sentence that caught my attention. He said:
The North Atlantic treaty was an engagement which was quite unprecedented for the United States-it was quite unprecedented for the United States to make that kind of long-range alliance with other countries. That was directly contrary to our earlier policies which had been pursued for over 100 years.
Yet we are living in an age when the United States has changed that policy, is taking an active part in international affairs, is stationing her forces overseas, and has been carrying on shoulder to shoulder with us ever since she entered world war II.
50433-28J
North Atlantic Treaty
Then consider, as the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) characterized it the other day, that courageous step by Great Britain. We know from the history of Great Britain that her policy was to have no commitments on the continent of Europe in the way of stationing troops there in any permanent sense; yet look at what has happened now. I think this was the great and decisive action of the London conference, the offer by Sir Anthony Eden that British troops would remain on the continent and would not be withdrawn unless under the most difficult and unexpected circumstances. Sir Anthony Eden, in the course of his statement at that conference, said this:
My colleagues will realize that what X have announced-
He was referring to the announcement that British troops would remain in Europe.
-is for us a very formidable step to take. You will know that ours is above all an island story. We are still an island people in thought and tradition, whatever the modern facts of weapons and strategy may compel. And it has been not without considerable reflection that the government which X represent here has decided that this statement could be made to you this afternoon.
That is leadership of a high order. I had hoped that Canada might have made as forthright a statement with regard to her forces in Europe as is implied in the commitment of Great Britain and the statement by Mr. Dulles. My hope is that nevertheless we shall remain solidly with Great Britain and the United States in this great commitment overseas. That, to me, has overshadowed this so-called rearming of Germany. Here we have the leading democratic nations in the world linked more closely together than ever before in their history, changing their centuries-old methods of dealing with foreign countries, the United States reversing a policy maintained for over 100 years, Great Britain reversing a policy maintained during all of her history in modern times, and both united with us and other countries in that great organization, NATO.
To bring Germany into that organization under these conditions, to forget some of the injuries of the past, to attempt to hold out the hand of friendship to Germany and to expect in return the hand of friendship from Germany-surely that is a great forward step in international relations. That is why I said at the beginning that I propose to support the motion now before us, and I support it with minor reservations. I was going to say without any reservations whatsoever, but they are extraordinarily minor because, as I see the picture, it is one of the most important steps that have been taken in the history of the world since the formation of NATO.

North Atlantic Treaty
I recall those words of Sir Winston Churchill contained in his history of the second world war. You remember them: In war, resolution; in defeat, defiance; in victory, magnanimity; in peace, good will.
This is a period when we can show magnanimity to Germany and greet her in the company of the NATO nations with good will.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF PROTOCOL ON ACCESSION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like most other speakers who have taken part in the debate I want to deal mainly with the military aspects of these agreements, and especially with the problem of rearming Germany; because that seems to be the part of the agreements that has caused the most worry and upset among many people throughout the country.
Since it was indicated that it was intended to bring this matter before the house I have received dozens of letters and cards not only from people in my own riding but from all over Canada protesting against the acceptance of these agreements. Granted that many of them came from communists and fellow travellers, nevertheless a good many of them, probably the majority, came from people who are good, honest, sincere citizens and who are motivated only by the deepest concern as to what the result may be.
I share that concern. I am greatly concerned about what may happen with respect to the rearming of Germany. My memory is not so short but what I can look back to the five years I spent fighting these same Germans. I have not forgotten the good friends whom I lost during that war. Nor have I forgotten the cries of men who were wounded, hurt, dying or drowning. I have not forgotten the sound of the whistle of German bullets nor the whistle of their bombs. I can still remember vividly the white wake of their torpedoes and the dull boom as they struck merchant ships. More than that, I can remember the hours I spent digging in the rubble, with my hands bleeding, trying to get civilian survivors out of the bomb ruins in London. I can remember an overturned lifeboat floating on the water, riddled with machine gun bullets. These things are not easy to forget. When we recall that we have gone through this ordeal twice in one lifetime, it makes it doubly hard to forget.
I am not too sure how far Germany can be trusted. I am not too sure how far her leaders can be trusted. But let us remember this, that not too many years ago practically every nation which is a signatory to the Paris agreement was an aggressor nation. This is true of Great Britain and France and all of them. Gradually these nations have

developed beyond this idea of using aggression to become a world power. Gradually they have become more and more willing to co-operate with the other nations of the world. I am hoping events will prove that Germany has reached that point and will co-operate fully with the western nations.
As I said, I am not too sure how far we can trust Germany. However, we know we cannot trust the communists. For years their leaders have been telling us that their ultimate aim is world domination and nothing less will suffice. They have even explained the ways and means by which they are going to attain this end, as the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) put on the record yesterday. Let us not forget, too, that Germany is split in half. One half of Germany is already armed and ready to take part in any move against the western nations. If we cannot trust West Germany, then we cannot trust East Germany any further; and we already have East Germany on the wrong side of the fence, fully armed and ready to go. They are being pushed by the communist forces stationed there.
We have the safeguards laid down in the agreements. I do not know whether they are adequate. After reading the protocols and listening to the minister yesterday, I have been relieved of a good many of the fears I had prior to that time. One thing that strikes me is the guarantee given by West Germany that she will not use arms for the unification of Germany or any other expansion of her borders.
Yesterday the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked about the manufacture of arms outside of Germany. They brought to the attention of the minister the aircraft plant that is being established in Spain by a German arms company. I believe that is fairly well covered because protocol IV, article 7, deals with the setting up of an agency to investigate the importation of arms and the amount of arms stored within West Germany. I cannot see how it would be possible, therefore, for any nation to rearm, maintain arms, or import arms without that fact coming to the attention of this agency.
It should be noted also that article 10 of protocol IV gives the necessary control so far as atomic armaments are concerned. I shall not read the protocol because it is too long, and I notice it is getting close to six o'clock.

The letters I have received have opposed the rearmament of Germany because it was felt it might interfere with the ultimate reunion of free Germany. I do not think that would be so, because Russia is not going to agree to any union until that suits her purposes. Russia is not going to allow free elections for some time at least because she knows it would not be possible to win a majority. The Russians know they could not win in West Germany, because the elections held there have already proven decisively that the people of West Germany have no intention of embracing communism. When you recall that West Germany contains the larger population of the two sections, it becomes even more doubtful that the Russians would agree to free elections in the near future.
In addition they know they cannot possibly win a free election in East Germany, in spite of the brainwashing and educational programs they have introduced. East Germany, for one thing, is mainly Catholic and the Catholics are noted for being one of the strongest groups opposed to communism. What guarantee have we that free elections will ever be held in Germany when the Russians will not allow their own people within the Soviet union to have free elections? How can they be expected to hold free elections in any protectorate, as a result of which they might lose power in that section of the country?
This afternoon I was glad to hear the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) give some idea of the cooperation extended by the Soviet union in the debates of the United Nations this year. My experience in the United Nations a year ago showed me how unwilling the Russians were to co-operate at that time with the western nations in working out some sort of formula for the reduction of arms and for peace.
Many of those who oppose these agreements do so because they feel that we are going to turn the communists against us. They seem to feel that by backing down we are going to gain favour, that because the strength of the Soviet union is continually growing we should become weaker. They probably feel that if we get weak and puny the communists will take pity on us, as we might take pity on a puppy.
Let us not fool ourselves. They have no pity in their make-up. The stronger they become and the weaker we become, the less chance we have of ever achieving peace on this earth, except on their terms. It is also said that because there is danger of a third
North Atlantic Treaty
world war which could entail the end of civilization, we should grovel at the feet of the communist aggressor and submit to slavery without doing anything to protect ourselves.
I do not think an arms race is the only solution. I agree with some hon. members who have said we should make a continued effort towards peaceful negotiations. I agree also with those who said that we should be sending more clothing, food and so on to the have-not peoples of the earth, because if we had shown to those underdeveloped people a few years ago any of that Christian charity we boast about, they would not be embracing communism today. And had we shown a bit of respect, a bit of charity toward the Chinese people in the thirties, we would not have had men facing them in Korea during the last few years, and standing by to protect themselves from the Chinese at the present time. But we made those mistakes, and at least partially because of that we have to keep the arms race going at full pace today.
Like some other hon. members who have spoken I agree that these agreements and the rearming of Germany can put us in a much stronger bargaining position, because strength and force represent the only language the communists understand. And if we can add 1,350 fighter planes, 500,000 men, and other armament to our forces it will greatly enhance our bargaining position.
We realize that there is a definite risk, but we must also remember that the continued occupation of West Germany could do nothing more than antagonize the people and drive them directly into the hands of the communists. No one likes to walk down a street in a town and see members of the armed forces of strange nations patrolling those streets and sharing the livelihood of that nation. They do not like it. People like to feel that they are free. It is much better for us to give them an opportunity to show their good will toward us and to show that they are willing to co-operate with us than to antagonize them to the point where we know very well we cannot hope for any peace with them.
I cannot see that we have any choice other than that of rearming Germany. Because, believe me, if it ever came to a hot war between us and the communists I would rather have the German fighting strength as an ally than as an enemy. I might as well be frank enough to say that my decision to support this motion was to some degree influenced by the fact that there is going to be no real widening of Canadian commitments. But it does make it possible for the

North Atlantic Treaty
Germans to help protect themselves, if the Russian hordes ever should pour across the border. Let us remember, too, that even if Germany does remain unarmed, Canada is committed to protect West Germany against invasion. Even if this entailed further commitments I would still feel justified in supporting the motion.
I think every Canadian having full knowledge of the facts would give support; because what we need now, in the light of all the facts, is plenty of determination, and to show that we are willing to back up that determination with acts of courage. I think, too, that any of those who think there is no war at the present time could not do better than read the article written by David Lawrence in the U.S. News and World Report of January 21. I am not going to read it, but I commend it to all members who think we are living in a period of peace. It deals with the border clashes in Indo-China, the bombing raids on nationalist China, the invasion of some of the nationalist islands along the Chinese coast, and so on. This article makes it perfectly clear that, in spite of the communist peace propaganda, there is an act of aggression taking place somewhere in the world every day. We have to arm ourselves against that, no matter how much we dislike doing so.
I support the motion, not because I want war; I do not. I hate it; but I hate slavery more.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF PROTOCOL ON ACCESSION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I start on the main part of my speech I want to refer for a moment to one remark of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) in a speech which I thought was otherwise an able one, when he expressed opposition to the proposal now before the house on the ground that the Canadian people were not very enthusiastic about it. As I heard him say that I could not help but remember the story of an American advertising man who was sent up to Canada to do a big job, to put on a big advertising campaign. After he had been up here for about a year he gave up the job in disgust because, he said, he never could get the Canadian people to think in terms of "greatest in the world" or "biggest in the world". He said the utmost in enthusiasm that he could ever get out of the Canadian people was "not too bad". I believe

the Canadian people will say of this proposal that is before us tonight, "not too bad".
If you will forgive a personal word, Mr. Speaker, apart altogether from the substance of what is before us in this motion, I want to say how proud I am to give my support to my oldest personal friend in the house, the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I am sorry that my second oldest friend in the house, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), is not here also because, while I do not always see completely eye to eye with him, I do greatly regret that he is not here to make his personal contribution to this discussion on what seems to me to be the most important decision likely to come before this parliament of Canada for a good many years.
We have heard a good many arguments pro and con, and it must be very obvious to anyone who knows the facts that there is a great deal of concern in the minds of the Canadian people as to what is the right course of action of this Canadian nation and this Canadian parliament, which is the servant of the Canadian nation. I frankly confess that in the past few months I have given the question my own deepest personal thought, and partly to clarify my own thinking on it I went back to London just a few weeks ago. I got to London on the 1st day of September, and the first sight that greeted my eyes in that great city was great billboards put up by the Conservative baron, Lord Beaverbrook, blazing out to all the city "Don't rearm Germany".
Because I myself was going to NATO headquarters to discuss some of the military facts and political problems connected with NATO I decided that to clarify my own thinking I would do what I had never been able to do since 1918, namely revisit some of the old battlefields of the first world war. I had the privilege of going from London to Paris and being driven to the old battlefields of Flanders, Vimy Ridge and the Somme. And, Mr. Speaker, by one of those unbelievable coincidences that sometimes happen to us, I spent the night in Arras at the foot of Vimy Ridge in an ancient hotel which somehow or other looked familiar to me. When I checked up next morning I found it was the very casualty clearing station to which I had been carried on September 2, 1918, with a blue cross on my forehead which they tell me means that you are not supposed to get better. But here I am, how many years later-I am not good at arithmetic, but anyway quite a few years later-still carrying around in my carcass, shall we say, some of the bits of good German steel that landed there on September 2, 1918. The Secretary

of State for External Affairs complains about his voice trouble. People sometimes complain that my voice is too harsh, but if they do I say "Oh, well, the reason is that my tongue is literally edged with bits of German steel which have been there for 37 years."
When you approach at night from the rear that beautiful monument which is a great credit to this Canadian nation, with a full harvest moon highlighting those two pylons reaching to the sky, I do not know what you think but I know what I thought. I thought it was like the arms of a bereaved woman reaching up to heaven in prayer as if to say "How long, O Lord, how long!" Then in the daylight you see that immense battlefield. You see on the foot of that monument the names of 11,000 Canadians whose bodies were never found, 11,000 of the 60,000 Canadians who paid the price in the first world war. Then when you look around you see equally great numbers of names of British troops, of French troops and French colonials. Above all, Mr. Speaker, when you go down to that immense cemetery where the bodies of the slain Germans are buried two to one under painted wooden crosses and check up the figures you find that 44,037 German servicemen are buried there. You look at the two stone monuments erected by German regiments between the two world wars, and when you walk up close to one of those monuments you see marks of bullets on it from German machine guns of the second world war.
Then, Mr. Speaker, no one needs to tell you we are dealing with a very serious problem indeed when we are dealing with German rearmament. But when you drive away from Vimy Ridge on those wonderful national highways built I think by Napoleon-but for all I know perhaps originally built by the Romans and rebuilt by Napoleon-and find that young boys who are working on those roads, when they see the Canada sign on your car, wave at you and say, "Canada bonne, Canada bonne", it gives you a nice warm feeling. It does stir you a bit, and you realize that probably they are the sons or grandsons of the Frenchmen of the generation you knew.
Then, Mr. Speaker, you drive a little further en route to Paris and through the city of Bapaume. In the main square which so many of us knew during the battle of the Somme in the first world war you see that very striking statue of a recumbent figure. When you get up to read the inscription under that recumbent figure, you see that it memorializes the mayor of the city of Bapaume who was shot during the second world war for not having called off the resistance of the
North Atlantic Treaty
civilians to the German occupation. Then when your guide, a former Liberal member of this very parliament who is good on history, tells you that the Germans also shot the mayor of Bapaume in the first world war, no one needs to tell you, even if they did before, that this German problem is a very real problem indeed.
I want tonight, Mr. Speaker, in the clearest terms of which I am capable, to try to demolish one of the greatest of the fallacies which are sometimes bandied about. I frankly confess that I am appalled when people write me such things as "Never again trust the Germans" and "No guns for the Huns". I say that I am appalled when people talk as if all Germans by race, by blood, by ancestry, were incurably evil. I do not know what this house thinks, but the more I think of it the more I believe that particular theory is just Hitlerism in reverse. It is just the most vicious form of racialism, just as it was vile and foul for Hitler to convince the German people that they were the master race, that they were superior creatures and that all the rest of the world were lesser species. I think it is just as vicious to take the view now that all Germans are incurably bad and that the German people should never be able to live their own lives again.
But there is an even more immediate reason, I think, why that doctrine should be rejected by this house. Where would we be in regard to our own beloved royal family if we adopted the theory that all Germans were incurably evil? What about the Mount-battens? Where would we be in regard to our very great friend President Eisenhower of the United States or General Gruenther, the great military head of our NATO coalition? Or if we want to come closer to home, where would we be in regard to some, including one from my own province, very fine generals in the Canadian army in both world wars? And where would we be with regard to the very fine people of Waterloo county or the people of German origin who have served us faithfully in this parliament and in all previous parliaments since and before federation?
The problem with which we deal is not the problem of evil Germans as a people. We are dealing with Germany as a great national power which perhaps has been something of a problem because she came too late on to the stage of history. She came later on the stage of power politics and history than some other nations, but I submit that the theory that Germany is an essentially evil warmongering power is a theory which hardly stands up in history.

North Atlantic Treaty
I hold in my hand an original copy of the London Times which reported the battle of Waterloo in the year 1815. As a truthful newspaperman I am bound to say that in these four pages of the London Times published in 1815 there is much more news than in our newspapers of today running to perhaps 96 pages.
I see in the main item, which by the way did not make the front page because that page was all taken up with advertisements, that the Duke of Wellington was reporting on the battle of Waterloo, and it states that he pinned the whole battle of Waterloo on the attack of the Prussians. The whole purport of his dispatch was that if it had not been for the Prussians as well as the British, Napoleon never would have been overthrown and the history of our times would have been very different indeed.
When I hear people say that the Germans are incurably evil, that there is no hope for the Germans and that a German should never be trusted with anything stronger than a cap pistol or a water pistol, I wonder if that stands up in the perspective of history. I have in my hand an extract from a book written by Professor Quincy Wright of the University of Chicago. This is a massive two-volume study of war from 1480 to 1941, roughly between the time of the discovery of America and the second world war.
On looking at the score card I find Germany pretty nearly at the end of the list for the number of wars fought. To be precise, I find that Germany is fourth from the end in the list of all the powers. I will give you, Mr. Speaker, or any member in this house one guess as to the names of the two nations that head this list of the number of wars fought, because 99 per cent of the members in this house are descendants of either one or the other. The first is Great Britain with 78 wars and the second is France, which is very close behind with 71 wars. Germany is a mere piker, small-time stuff in the light of history and the matter of fighting wars.
The man who wrote this book is a very modest American. He seems to take great delight out of the fact that in 150 years the United States of America was engaged in only 13 wars; but then he puts down one of those little stars, those things they call an asterisk, and he has a note indicating that this does not include 110 expeditions against the Indians.
I think the real problem with which our generation has to deal, and with which this house is called upon to deal now, is that of the terms on which Germany is to regain her freedom of action in the family of
[Mr. Phllpott.l
nations. I have never, even in the worst and most bigoted days of the war, been among those who thought we could keep Germany down permanently by force. We tried to keep her down by force before, and we got Hitler. We can never keep Germany down perpetually by force. Those people who talk about keeping Germany disarmed forever are simply stating in another way that they think Germany should be deprived of selfgovernment forever.
I have made quite a study of the statements of the social democratic party in Germany, for which party I have great respect, and I have never seen any statement by that party which did not indicate very plainly that once they regained their unity, once they regained their self-government, they themselves would decide in their own interests to what level they should rearm. It seems to me that what we are called upon here to decide is upon what terms Germany is going to be given the right of self-government, and on what terms Germany is going to be given the right to rearm to a limited extent.
I confess frankly that had history taken another course; had the war come to an end; had we got first a Germany united and peaceful and willing to conduct itself, shall we say, as a greater Switzerland; had we got a united and peaceful Europe, including everything west of Russia, willing to conduct itself as a still greater Switzerland, then in my opinion everything would have been happier for all concerned. But we cannot make the waters of history run uphill. We are in our present position, and it is not an imaginary position indeed.
I referred at the outset of my speech to the fact that I had the great privilege of going to NATO headquarters. I happened to be there when Sir Anthony Eden was doing his great peace-making job, picking up the pieces of what had been wrecked through the destruction of EDC, in my opinion in a great, historic, adventurous and faithful way -faithful in the very sense of the word, full of faith. We faced tragedy at that moment. But I saw Sir Anthony Eden sitting on a bench with Premier Mendes-France. I didn't know what they were discussing, because I saw them only from a distance; but I think at that moment history was being made.
Then on the front page of every newspaper in Paris that afternoon I saw the picture of John Foster Dulles and Chancellor Adenauer studiously posed at a meeting in Germany. I do not think the French people are very slow on the uptake. I think every French person knew perfectly well what was the choice for the entire western

community at that moment. It was "Either let us get together; let us weld western unity; let us stand together; let us make the best arrangement we can, or else." As certainly as we are here today we would have been faced with a straight two-way alliance between the United States and Germany. Had that happened, then in my opinion we soon would have been faced with the proposal General de Gaulle was brooding about; that is, a counter-alliance between France and the Soviet union, and we thee, would have been further on the road to a third world war than we are today.
I sometimes wonder who will go down in history as the greatest peacemaker this country has every produced. It may be our present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). History will speak very highly of him, and of all of us who are members of parliament and members of the government at the time of making this decision. If this decision turns out well, history will say we were wise people indeed. But if this great decision turns out badly history will say we were ill-advised indeed. Unfortunately none of us has the faculty of being able to peer with uncanny accuracy into the future. At any time we can only do our best with the light the good Lord has given us.
From our own North American history I draw a great lesson. If you go to the town of Deseronto in the county of Hastings and look in the main square you will not find any monument to the greatest person ever born in that town; but for many years I have made a hobby of the study of North American Indian history, and I believe that a man who was born in the town of Deseronto was the greatest and most practical peacemaking statesman this world has yet produced.
If you dig through the dusty tomes in the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, or read the annals stored in the archives at Albany, New York, you will find the history of this great Indian peacemaker, whose name was Deganawida, and who spent 12 years of his life in welding together the original five-nation Indian confederacy. Those were the five hostile tribes who for hundreds of years had been just as bloody and warlike as the great powers of our own century.
When at last his great statesmanlike effort was crowned with victory and representatives of the original five nations, who had been bitter enemies, were gathered together in a building, they sat down together for six whole days before anyone said anything. I sometimes think the United Nations would have got on a lot better if we had waited a little longer before we began to talk in the
North Atlantic Treaty
hostile and belligerent terms so often used in the past 10 years.
The original five-nation Indian confederacy was eventually broadened to include a sixth Indian group, and this six-nation Indian confederacy kept the peace absolutely by banishing the anarchy and lawless relationship that had existed between these former enemies for hundreds of years.
I for one, Mr. Speaker, believe that what was done by the six-nation Indian confederacy in North America hundreds of years ago is not beyond the possibility of achievement in our time. If we have anything in our Canadian history of which we can be justifiably proud-and sometimes I think we should not be too proud of it because neither part of our nation sought this destiny-it is that people from two great countries in Europe which for hundreds of years had been the bitterest of enemies and at one time fought a series of wars lasting a hundred years, now live together in perfect amity. Our greatest achievement is that we have enabled people of two races, two cultures, and two languages to live side by side in this great country and work together as partners to make a united Canada which is highly regarded by every nation on this earth.
I am not one of those who believe there is anything peculiar about the French and English, or that there is anything unique about their respective qualities. But I believe that the process which worked to enable the people of French and English origin to live together could possibly work also to include all the nations of the western alliance who have been allies in former wars. I believe also that that very process and that same approach will yet bring us great friends and great assets in the German people.
If you will forgive me for a personal reference, Mr. Speaker, I would like to recall that one of my brothers went off to the United States after the first world war. He heard that members of one branch of the family came from Ireland, and another branch instead of coming to Canada went down into Kentucky. But much to his chagrin, when he went down to look up our relatives he found they had been the worst feuding, fighting lawbreakers in the entire state of Kentucky, up to a certain point. When he delved into their short history he found that some wise person at the proper stage of historical development had found a way of making these lawless, feuding, fighting people fit into the law-abiding picture. His formula was very simple. He just made them policemen.

North Atlantic Treaty
I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, there is anything in the nature of the German people or anything in the nature of Germany as a country which makes it inevitable that Germany will again cause trouble. In saying that I am not unaware of the risks everyone has pointed to in regard to this arrangement. One risk I see very clearly is that at some future time the rearming of Germany might bring about again what Ludendorff did with Lenin in 1917, or what Hitler did with Stalin in 1939. But I think there are risks in any course of action or inaction open to us.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that when human beings are faced with a decision which depends on whether they take an outlook which is full of faith or full of doubt, when their decision depends on whether or not they are going to rely on the good will of another aggregation of human beings or are going to take for granted that this other aggregation will act for the worst, on the basis of ill will, we can never take a better guide as to what our decision should be than words of the illustrious Sir Wilfrid Laurier, when he said in almost the last speech he ever made:
Let me tell you that for the solution of these problems you have a safe guide, an unfailing light, if you remember that faith is better than doubt and love is better than hate.
It is in that spirit that I for one am proud to stand here tonight and say that with my eyes wide open, having a firm conviction of faith in the good will of Germany, having faith in the progressive organization of humanity towards a basis of international and world law, I shall cast my vote in support of the agreements which are before us tonight.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF PROTOCOL ON ACCESSION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased with the tone of the debate thus far. it has been conducted with a seriousness which I think is worthy of the occasion. I note that the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) has been able to follow on this occasion the entertaining and humorous vein he usually pursues. At least the debate has been serious enough that no attacks have been made upon those who have presented views contrary to those expressed by other speakers, and I propose to adopt the same course. I shall not even try to refute contrary arguments. I shall, at the risk of repetition, perhaps, say some things which have already been said. I shall advance conclusions to which I had come before the matter was mooted at all in this place and which I had previously jotted down to clarify my own thinking. These points I do not think I shall even embellish or elaborate.
The private member of parliament is at a disadvantage when discussing foreign affairs. He has, particularly if he belongs to a smaller


party in the house, no research facilities, and has had no opportunity to make contacts with the leaders of opinion in other countries throughout the world. He has to rely very largely for the formation of his own opinions on what he reads of the opinions of others; and what he reads may, as we have discovered, be mixed with a good deal of propaganda of one kind or another.
But after all a private member of parliament does have some feelings. He has, I hope, at least a modicum of common sense, and he does represent in a way the collective good sense of those who sent him to this place. Many people think, and this is proven by the letters we have received and the interviews we have had with people either at home in our own constituencies or since we have come here, that the opinion of a member of parliament like myself or the opinion of an opposition group such as we constitute here, can have some effect upon the ultimate decision as to the ratification of these agreements, including the rearming of Germany. On that point, as I have perhaps vainly tried to explain to them, they are quite wrong.
I think the people of the country should know that Canada was committed to the ratification of these agreements months ago. We are here discussing foreign policy after- and I emphasize the word "after"-rather than before the event. More and more the foreign policy of Canada is decided by the Department of External Affairs and, I think it is fair to say, less and less by parliament as time goes on. That department in its dealings with the diplomats of other countries shows complete assurance that anything it chooses to do, even months ahead, will later be endorsed by the government majority in the house; and that is so on this present occasion.
The protocol will be ratified. Rearmament of Germany will be ratified. I speak with assurance, particularly in view of the ratification by the French national assembly under pressures which I shall not discuss here. All we can do here is subscribe to a fait accompli or refuse to subscribe to it; and for myself, I refuse so to subscribe. With full consciousness of the ultimate futility of my action, a futility which I think I have explained, certainly to my own satisfaction, so far as its effect is concerned, I shall vote against this proposal. Under the circumstances I realize the futility of making a long speech about it, and I am not going to do so.

In the consideration of this matter one could be swayed by his emotions if he allowed his emotions to get the better of his reason. I suppose, Mr. Speaker, that all of us, even the wise men, are swayed by emotions whether or not we know it. So far as emotion is concerned, one could quote the words of the great statesmen of the period of the last war and the justified vituperation that was directed against our nazi enemies. I have a recollection of Mr. Churchill hissing into the radio-those nazis. "Never again" was the slogan. May I remind you, sir, that never is a long, long time; and as to the "again" it is here with us. Today we have come to "again".
Another emotion that might be aroused in us springs out of the communist opposition in this country to German rearmament. I said that in my opinion the debate up to the present had been carried on in a serious and dignified manner, but I should like to make one exception. I refer to the rather snide remark-I do not like the word but I cannot think of a better one at the moment-of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who suggested that there might have been some softening of our opinion or the opinion of the country in this regard on account of certain propaganda from the handful of communists in Canada. It is true that the minister immediately withdrew that inference in so far as members of parliament were concerned. I have heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) do that sort of thing before. I believe, however, that inferences, accusations or slander once indulged in can never be completely withdrawn. I am sorry to have to interject that note, but I think the method which has become so familiar to the members of this house was fairly evident in the debate this afternoon.
Speaking for myself I might say my natural reaction to the opposition which has been expressed by a handful of communists in this country, if it tended to drive me in any direction, would persuade me to support ratification if I were not otherwise so inclined. But I am not going to allow a handful of communists in this country, or a mob of people in this country, to form my opinion for me. I do not admire the intelligence of people who would fall into that particular type of trap. The communists, as I have discovered, are difficult people with whom to live. Every time I have sought re-election they have opposed me. As I say, I am not going to fall into the trap of being swayed by the opinion of anyone else. I must stand on my own.
North Atlantic Treaty
Translating this idea of living with them, or to use a phrase that has now become rather trite, coexistence with communists, I may say it now has a wider meaning. We shall probably find it rather difficult to live with the communist nations; that is my own reaction. Distasteful as it may be to live with them, however, I think we would find it even more distasteful to die with them. This may be strong language, but in my opinion that will be the ultimate result if war, in its full force, breaks out amongst us. But enough of emotion.
I have said that we must be ruled by reason. I am opposed to the ratification of this protocol, which includes the rearmament of Germany, for the following among many other reasons which I could but shall not elaborate. I want my statement to be clear so that he who runs may read, and so there may be no doubt as to what my opinions are.
I believe that the rearmament of Germany now will be an irrevocable step in dividing that country, and will create an impassable barrier to the unification of that country. I believe it would be considered a warlike step, rather than as some of my friends on the other side have suggested, a peaceful gesture. I believe it is as a warlike gesture that it will be considered by what one might call the neutralist countries and particularly those in Asia, those countries that are watching us closely for the implementation of our oft-professed desire for peace.
I believe, in common with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), that time is an important element. It is important in one way he did not mention. If it is granted to us, time will provide the opportunity for a new generation of German youth, unarmed over a period of years and living under peaceful conditions, to arise. This generation would be less military-minded than the generation preceding it. If we begin now once more to put German youth into military uniforms we will interrupt the impact of a period of peace upon the youth of Germany.
I believe further that the rearmament of Germany would be the ultimate step in completing the division of the eastern and western worlds into opposing camps. I believe that the rearmament of Germany to the extent of 12 divisions would be futile, because such action would only be reciprocated by the creation of an equal, double or triple if you like, force on the other side. The other side would have the advantage of manpower, and we should be merely accelerating the pace of the military armament race. In any event I do not believe

North Atlantic Treaty
12 German divisions, even if it may be assumed that they would be used on the side of the west-a point in regard to which some speakers in this house today have been uncertain-would make any essential difference in a total war. Military leaders such as Viscount Montgomery, General Gruenther, and a United States admiral whose name I can never recall, have expressed the view that there is no doubt in their minds that should war break out, thermonuclear and atomic weapons would be used. I ask you whether you believe 12 divisions will shift the balance in favour of the western world.
I believe that the creation of further divisions-this is something we should listen to and think about-proves that we are still clinging to the fantastic and obsolete idea that differences between the peoples of the world can in fact be settled through force of arms, and that one side can emerge victorious. I do not believe that war is inevitable. Somehow I have that faith. It is backed, I believe, by reasons which I could state if I desired to take the time. I do not believe that any of the people in this world want war. I do believe that all the peoples of the world want peace. The rearming of further legions looks to me like a peculiar way of expressing that desire for peace.
I am not sufficiently optimistic to believe that if you did grant Germany permission to create 12 new divisions, the creation of those 12 divisions would lessen the difficulty of control. Rather it would increase it. If conditions do not change, Germany is going to arm herself. Let us make no mistake about that. She will rearm, and that rearmament will be limited only by her own desires. But we need not thrust arms upon her.
I am aware that the nations of the western world have ratified these agreements. I am aware, too, that some parliaments, some under severe pressure, some by small majorities, and some by devious means, have ratified them. History has proved that on occasions the majority has been wrong, even an enthusiastic majority, as my friend the Minister of National Health and Welfare has this afternoon-and quite wrongly, in my opinion -described the majority of nations supporting this protocol. But history has proved, as I said, that the majority may be wrong.
This government has set its mind upon ratification. Even this government, at times, has been wrong, and I believe it is wrong now. I must assume my own responsibility, and when doing so I do not speak for this group or for any other members of this group,
	*
but speak only for myself. And I speak as I believe. I must speak and I must vote as I believe, and I must oppose ratification.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF PROTOCOL ON ACCESSION OF FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I never thought it would become necessary to rise in this House of Commons in a debate of this kind, but I have been greatly surprised to hear some hon. members opposite take part in the campaign in which we, in this parliament, have been asked to vote against the rearmament of Germany.
It is in the light of the grim facts that we are forced to do so. But has Russia helped the world since 1945 to make us change our minds? I have been surprised in this House of Commons, in this parliament where freedom is our goal, to hear some hon. members speak against something which is a necessity in the life of this country as well as in the lives of those countries which, with us, are devoted to liberty and freedom.
Yesterday I listened to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and I was greatly pleased with the manner in which he placed before the house the fact that today against our own will, we are confronted with the necessity of rearming Germany because Russia and her satellites are ranged against us. I read the minister's speech of January 1 in which he said that we have to do this, and that our people should not forget that the rearmament of Germany comes within the framework of a world organization in which the North Atlantic nations are united.
So Germany will be rearmed, and within what scope? We have developed the treaty of the North Atlantic nations, and under the procedure now being taken, Germany will be incorporated within a group of nations organized not for the purpose of waging war but rather that of waging peace. And this is something which Russia and her satellites have not done since 1945.
What about Poland? Is it not a fact that Poland was always an enemy of Russia? Yet Russia took Poland and we see that today Poland, without the consent of her own people, is obliged to suffer the reorganization of that country by Russia, with the Polish people having no right to say one word in the matter.
When we seek to rearm Germany we are criticized by some of our friends on the other side of the house. When we seek to rearm Germany to bring peace to the world we are criticized by some people, the same people who are satisfied when Russia rearms Poland, a country which over the centuries has been Russia's enemy. If hon. members opposite could give me any explanation of the stand they take, perhaps I would be prepared to

discuss the matter with them. But the fact today is that while Poland is rearmed by Russia, the people of Poland have had nothing to say about it.
Because of events since 1945 we have reached the point where we are forced to rearm Germany. This does not give us any pleasure, but we must keep in mind that as individuals we do not run the world. The world as it is today is the result of history, and history records that at times we have had to fight while at other times we have been able to get together. But we have to get together by peaceful means, by agreement and understanding. That is not what Russia has done since 1945. We are doing our best to build a world in which peace will govern the actions of each individual. I say it is a bad thing for Canada when, within this country, such campaigns as I have indicated have been promoted.
It may be that this is done in good faith. I will not question the good faith of those who are behind it. But these are the people who come to us and say, "Do not do anything. Be gentle. Be nice. Let it go. You know, Russia and communism do not carry with them any harm against any country or any people."
This is a bad position to take, because those citizens who undertake the campaign do not serve our faith in democracy, they do not carry out our faith in idealism, or our faith in freedom and liberty.
When I see some of my friends on the other side, who are always promoting the freedom of human beings on earth, working against themselves when they do not agree with us on the rearmament of Germany-because the rearmament of Germany is one solution which will create peace in the world-I am amazed. If we can get more countries to come on our side we can be sure that one day we shall convince those people who do not think as we do that there is only one way to build a peaceful world. That is: to give freedom to all men, women and children in every country in the world; to assure them freedom and liberty which will make them strong enough to change the form of their government, if the government is trying to subdue them under a form of dictatorship which is not good for any human being.
We are asked today not to rearm Germany, but to bring Germany within the nations which, since the implementation of the charter of the United Nations, are working very hard to bring about peace in this world. Can we get peace anywhere in the world if we are not sold on the idea that peace comes from our hearts and our minds? Do you think it
North Atlantic Treaty
is possible to create peace in any country in the world if you disturb the minds and the hearts of the people by trying to induce them to campaign against their own country, against peace and against a way to create peace? No, it is impossible; and no political ideas in this world will bring about peace if we do not get together in good faith and sincerity to promote peace in the world.
Peace is something formidable. Peace is something very difficult to understand. Peace is a relation between the life of any individual, anywhere, and his own country. Peace is something we carry in our hearts and our minds. I cannot understand why today some people in this country and in other countries are carrying on a campaign against peace for the benefit of the U.S.S.R. I have no criticism of their leaders; they might be acting in good faith.
What are the facts since 1945? We sacrificed our sons and ourselves, we sacrificed this country for the freedom of the world, and we were helping Russia in every way possible. Who would have thought at that time that after the victory was won we would be antagonizing ourselves over things which mean the destruction of the people's minds, because communism does not mean anything but the destruction of the people's minds.
They are building up in Russia today a mentality which does not appeal to the people but which is a form of obedience to their leaders and to the government which has no connection with the hearts and the activities of the people of that country. We want to keep our freedom to think, our freedom to pray to God, in which we have faith. We want to keep our liberty to do what we think is good for the country, and this is a resolution which might assure us that we are going to protect the free world against the forces of communism, the forces of Russia. We must remember this.
I do not care very much about what people might think. Liberty to think is the important thing. Of course we might use it for ends which are for the good of the country, or we might use our freedom for an end which has no relation to our own good. Canada is a country where we are free to think what we believe is the best for our country, what is best for humanity and what is best for the good behaviour of the people.
What have we received today from those who have spoken against this resolution which was so well presented by the Secretary of State for External Affairs? What have we? Nothing; just words, an expression of

North Atlantic Treaty
views, which might bring to the speakers a few votes or some sympathy. We have to be realistic. What is the world situation today? Russia has some bases in Prussia. She does not care about the sovereignty of Bulgaria and Roumania. Russia does not have any care for the sovereignty of Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia or even Austria today. It is a dragon with long arms trying to conquer the western world, and this fact does not seem to appeal to our friends who are talking against the rearmament of Germany. Look at what Russia is doing in Asia. It might have been possible for Russia to stop the Korean war, which cost the United States, Canada and the other free nations a great deal of money. What did Russia do to prevent that war? I would like someone to answer that question.

speechtext:
I am sure your answer would be no good. What did Russia and red China do to prevent the Indo-China war? When you tell me you will answer, it means to me that you are not free in your mind to give a free answer to my question.
We are facing difficulties. We are in a world where it is very difficult to balance the forces of one side and the forces of the other side, but there is one thing which cannot be contradicted by anyone; that is the fight between freedom and slavery. If Poland could rise and speak her mind she would not stay for one minute within the framework of what we call the satellites of Russia, because we know that the satellites of Russia are not free to express their will, their faith and their convictions.
It would be the same with any of the nations that are now subjugated by Russia. We have nothing personally against Russia. I do not want to antagonize any country in the world, because I have faith in the good will of the people of any country. I think it might be possible to bring the people of these countries together. We are told that if they could but understand the way we think, the way we feel and what we have in our hearts, they would join forces with us to establish a world of peace, a world of good will, a world which would be one of glory for our children, where war would be no more, where peace would dominate the minds of everyone.
I should like to say a few words in French before I conclude my remarks. We are told that we are rearming Germany.

(Translation) :
This is not quite the case. We are associating Germany with NATO, and when voting for German rearmament, I shall feel the same grief as my learned friend from Cartier (Mr. Crestohl).
One thing must not be forgotten in this world, and it is that those who speak or agitate are not always those who decide the fate of nations. History is stronger than the individual action that might be taken in a particular place, and the course that nations have to follow at one time of their history is determined by the forces of history. We are surprised to have to rearm Germany, but that is what history has always taught us. Napoleon fought against his foes and a few months later he was rearming them and fighting along with them. I could go further back in history, and say that the best friends of Louis XIV were his former enemies whom he had defeated.
But we must not forget that we are no longer living in a world where wars must be fought. We are living in a world where we must live in peace, where we must make peace. And this peace will only come from such personal feelings as we may have towards it. It is these personal feelings which we must ourselves have and spread abroad by word and thought.
Some countries want war, but the very basis of the United Nations is that the world must live in peace. Statements to this effect also occur in the charter of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Here, in Canada, we want peace, we are looking for peace. But peace is not a unilateral thing. It is achieved through agreements and the good will of nations working towards the same ends. Ever since 1945, every time that this country has thought it possible to seek an agreement with Russia, it has done so, not only for the good of our country but for that of every other nation. But Russia has always found a way of evading the issue, of delaying discussion and of preventing, by its actions, peace-loving nations from finding a solution.
I need not repeat the statement made yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). We know that in her relations with the rest of the world Russia does not act in good faith and that she endeavours to implant here, as in all other countries, a philosophy which tends to destroy individual liberty in order to allow her to dominate nations. Communism is but one form of the activities of the Soviet republic. The Soviet republic pursues the

age-old idea that Russia should dominate Europe. Peter the Great, imbued with this idea, led his armies across Poland and tried to conquer her. Russia nowadays pursues the same idea of world conquest envisioned by Peter I, Peter the Great, father of panslavism. The outcome of revolution was that the idea of the aristocracy and of the middle class became that of the mass of the people.
The error of the communists makes possible this spiritual distortion being spread about by individuals fascinated by this doctrine which destroys the human community. By an act both just and fair, any individual can secure what is best from a society based on freedom and justice. Is it not unfortunate to see some of our fellow citizens work counter to the principles accepted by this government and counter to our natural propensity to accept the only solution? In France, in England, in the United States, the government of the country is in agreement. However, some groups believe, in good faith or in bad, that it would be better to be slaves than free citizens. The liberty of our country to choose the best means of maintaining the marvellous conditions which exist in this country must prevail. Security, as well as liberty, is the undeniable right of everyone.
Oh, I know very well that we may have, on the right or left, political theories which are different. But when these theories are applied by men of good faith they never affect the security of the nation. I have nothing against those who have accepted them since they may make a contribution to the well-being, security and liberty of the nation by fair and constructive criticism.
But still, I would not like to see in this country any move which would tend to scuttle what we have managed to accomplish since the turn of the century for the Canadian people. But for us, in the province of Quebec, communism is the fundamental error of those who have no confidence in themselves. It is the fundamental error of those who believe in nothing save in submission to the dominating power of a government which ignores them. We in Quebec still have faith in those ideas which are the very basis of this Christian civilization of ours. And having faith in that civilization we are convinced that no force will destroy man in his faith, conscience and spirit. And those who think they can dominate us through what I call a spiritual nebula and which some call communism will never succeed in convincing those of our faith that they should accept being slaves rather than the free men that we are.
