speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it requires a good deal of self-assurance to believe that one can add anything to this debate, particularly considering the level at which it has been carried on and the ground it has covered.
But there are three reasons I wish to say something on this matter. First of all, because of the vast importance of the question we are discussing. Second, because I feel that with those who have announced they are going to vote against it I have very much in common. I go far along the same road, and I cannot help hoping that at the end of my remarks they will take the turn I am taking and not the one they have announced they are adopting. Third, I want to speak because I have had occasion in my own constituency to talk to deputations who visited me, and I feel I would like to put my views on record for their benefit and for the benefit of anyone else who may see these remarks.
It was rather shocking to me to find the amount of indoctrination to which these deputations had been subjected. Some of them, particularly a younger group, told me they considered President Eisenhower and Sir Winston Churchill warmongers. For that reason-and this is one of the excuses I have for taking part in this debate-I want to put on record quite briefly one or two of the things President Eisenhower has said, which seem to me to show that we are fortunate to have a man of such wide humanity in the responsible position in which he now finds himself.
He is describing the position he is in and the responsibility he carries, and he says: "... if we are going ... to take such a fateful decision as leads us one step toward war, let us, by no means, do it in response to our human emotions of anger and resentment, hut let's do it after we have prayerfully considered it and found, as (President Woodrow) Wilson expressed it, 'no other means of protecting our rights.' "
I want to put that on record because I think it is desirable that it should come to the attention of as many people as possible.
As to Sir Winston Churchill we know his record. We know that unworthy people for unworthy ends tried to represent him as a warmonger for election purposes. But we believe that has been long since swept away and he has appeared in his true light as a man whose whole desire at advanced age still is to do something for the cause of peace.
To the deputations that came to see me I made a very simple, perhaps naive answer.

North Atlantic Treaty
I said, "I will agree with you as to the danger. You do not have to argue with me, because there are dangers. But the best answer I can give you is the vote in the French chamber." Surely if any people in this world know the dangers it is the French. They have suffered again and again at the hands of the Germans, and if they can bring themselves to vote as they did surely the rest of us can do so also.
I pointed out to them that there are encouraging signs. I reminded them that the Germany which makes up West Germany is not the Prussia that we found so truculent and difficult. I reminded them that it was the milder Germans we were dealing with, the Germans for whom we used to have a friendly feeling as we faced them across no-man's land. When we found the Saxons there I think, if my memory serves me right, we were quite sympathetic, and we perhaps felt more irritated at divisional headquarters than we did at the Saxons.
There is reason to hope and believe that the democracy which failed to take hold in Germany between the two wars will take hold now. We believe Adenauer is serious and sincere. There is some ground for the belief that we may have a Germany which is not going to hand itself over to the military but is going to go out for peace.
I repeat that there is, of course, a risk in German rearmament. But in the case of Russian rearmament it is not a risk but a reality which we have with us now. That actuality is so real that I find it difficult to understand how my friends with whom I agree so much and with whom I go so far along the road apparently do not end up with me.
Now let us look back for a moment. Let us remind ourselves of our disarmament in 1945. Let us remind ourselves of our feelings during and after the war. Let us remind ourselves of the agonizing anxiety with which we followed the Russian campaign during the war. Let us remember the days of Stalingrad and how we agonized over what was going on then. Let us remember what Churchill said in 1941 when Hitler attacked the Russians. He said, "Whoever fights against Hitler is our friend." Let us remember the feelings we had in 1945 when we hoped that we were all going to co-operate in working for peace.
At this point I want to put on the record words used in the house by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) in March, 1949, at the time we were voting on NATO. Let me here remind the house that we had a practically unanimous vote for NATO, and let me venture to say that it is utterly impossible
[Mr. Macdonnell.l
for me to understand how anyone who voted for NATO can now vote against this resolution, because it seems to me that the arguments which prompted us then are just as strong now. What I shall read sets out well our pressing sense of disappointment at the end of the war when we found that the cooperation which we had hoped for was not forthcoming. At page 2072 of Hansard of March 28, 1949, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said:
Those of us who were at the San Francisco conference hoped and believed that the victorious nations would unite to prevent aggression, to end the threat of war, and to lay the foundations of that permanent peace for which men and women of good will hoped and prayed. But even whilst we were at San Francisco and the conference was in progress, indications were not lacking that understanding would be difficult.
Further on on the same page I read:
Shortly after that a Labour government was elected in Great Britain. As we know, they believed absolutely there was every possibility that they would be able to reach understandings with the Soviet union on basic problems. It was not long, however, until it became obvious that the communist government and its parties throughout the world had launched a vicious offensive against democratic socialist governments and their parties everywhere. Because of that and the bitter attacks on countries with democratic socialist governments, to which we listened with grave and growing concern at Lake Success in the autumn of 1946, it became evident that far greater difficulties faced the world than were anticipated at San Francisco.
We can recall so well, as if it were yesterday, that disappointment. We disarmed then with almost feverish haste, and we had it almost completed before we woke up to the fact that the communist countries were not following our example. Now we are told that we must work for disarmament again, and apparently we are to do it by unilateral disarmament. Apparently we are to negotiate from weakness. That is what I understood the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) to say, and it is so hard for me to understand. Surely if we have learned anything in these last years it is that the only time we have got anywhere is when we have negotiated not from weakness but from strength.
It seems to me that we can say, with all our imperfections and all the criticisms we make of ourselves-and we are able to criticize ourselves and each other in this free country-nobody outside of a lunatic asylum has any but the most whole-souled desire for peace. Incidentally, when I listened to those young people who came to see me and realized they had been poisoned with the thought that in this free country on this free continent, and in Britain and the other free countries, there was anyone who had other than a sincere desire for peace, I understood better

than ever before what evil subversive propaganda was at work. So I come back to say that we wish to work for peace. We wish to disarm, but surely we have learned the lesson that unilateral disarmament is no good.
I want to deal for a moment with the speech of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), whom I respect and whose speech yesterday I respected. But I suggest to him that he was not at his usual level of logical clear thinking. I read briefly from his words as found at page 395 of Hansard:
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich dares to hope that the hydrogen bomb is so terrible that it will not be used; therefore we must have conventional armaments upon which to rely. We all hope that is true, but I wonder whether in our heart of hearts any of us really believes that a third world war would go very long without the use not just of the obsolete atomic bomb but of thermonuclear weapons.
He went on to say:
... I feel we have to start from that premise and somehow we must take the kind of steps which will make sure that war will not break out again.
But these are the steps that those of us who are in favour of the resolution want to take. These steps are the ones we believe give us the best chance. We realize the dangers, but surely we are entitled to argue that we have tried to negotiate from weakness and we have found it no good. What small success we had in Korea surely was by reason of what Churchill called the "valiant decision" of Truman in 1950, and how valiant it was, to stand up to aggression at that time.
Incidentally, while the debate was going on it occurred to me to wonder whether if we heard next week that Germany had turned down this resolution we would be very happy about it.
The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) said we might just as well face the fact that Germany is going to rearm. I was amazed to hear him say that and at the same time announce that he was going to vote against the treaty. If Germany is going to rearm, would we not rather have them rearm and be on our side, be part of our team? I could hardly believe my ears when I heard that. We all recognize the danger. We all know that safeguards can never be 100 per cent complete, but surely we have to take calculated risks and go ahead.
I should also like to put on the record what seems to me a statement clear as crystal emanating from that great man-and he has become much greater this year by what he has done-Sir Anthony Eden, speaking in
North Atlantic Treaty
the British House of Commons on the 17th of November last. I cannot see any answer to this. He said:
What are the alternatives that now face Europe? In the main, there are only three. Either the cold war will continue; if so, we shall have a continuation of the heavy financial burdens, to which the right hon. gentleman the member for Ebbw Vale-
I hope if there are any Welshmen present they will correct my pronunciation.
- (Mr. Bevan) referred, over a period of years with all the strains and stresses . . . that that brings with it. The second possibility is that the cold war will become a hot war. If that happens, I do not think, with all respect, that the calculations of any of the treasuries of the world will become very important one way or the other. There is a third alternative which is that, out of these arrangements which we have so carefully built up, it may be possible for negotiations to be developed in Europe which may lead to ultimate success and agreement. It is for this third possibility that we are now working. We think that the Paris agreements have taken us some steps towards that . . . The only real alternative to accepting the Paris agreements would be to plunge the west into confusion and despair. Is anybody seriously going to contend we should better be able to negotiate with Soviet Russia if we were in that particular condition? I cannot believe that to be so.
I should like to say a word more about the French attitude. Some of us had a good deal to do with the French more years ago than we like to count, and we conceived for them the greatest admiration, respect and affection. We were able for that reason to sympathize with them, particularly when the second war came and, bleeding still from the scars of the first war, they were overwhelmed.
They are now facing a third time of trial. When I was in France four years ago I recall travelling on a train and sitting in a dining car opposite a French lady. When she found I came from Canada she said, "Canadians are a very fortunate people." One felt the bitter anxiety which they were facing every hour of their lives. The French have agreed to this. It is true the majority was small but, as the member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) pointed out, if you remove the communist vote the majority becomes substantial.
The last point I want to make is that we are told time is essential. I suppose time is always essential. Apparently what was meant by that argument, if I could understand it well, was that as time was essential we were to give more time for talks with Russia. We were not to sign this agreement because to sign it would make negotiations with Russia more difficult. We were, therefore, to give time and we were not to sign. I believe I have already said enough

North Atlantic Treaty
to indicate how utterly unsound that argument seems to be. Mr. Eden makes this point clear when he says:
Not for a moment do I accept the proposition that if these agreements are recognized, we have to give up hope of solving any of the issues of Europe today which affect soviet Russia ... X do not believe it for a minute. On the contrary, the fact that they are now in such a hurry to summon a conference that could not possibly meet in the time allotted is an indication of the fact that, if we proceed calmly and steadily with these proposals, we shall have better opportunities for negotiation than we have had for a very long time.
So, Mr. Speaker, I end where I began. We have two dangers and both of them are substantial. I like to think that the German danger is not as great as we imagine it. I like to associate myself with the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill). In spite of everything that happened during the last war, in spite of the bestialities inspired by Hitler, we all know that in a very real sense the great majority of the people in Germany are people who love and hate the same things that we love and hate.
The other danger is the Russian danger. I do not suppose for one moment that the individual Russians want war any more than we do, but they are in the grip of the forces of despotism. They can be turned to the purposes of a few men who may at any time act with a dreadful irresponsibility toward the human race. It seems to me, therefore, that while recognizing to the full all that has been said by those to the left, we come right back to a simple choice as to which of the two dangers is the greater. I know which I feel is the greater, and I shall vote for the resolution.

I rise, Mr. Speaker, to support the views expressed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre so ably and so clearly last evening. Like the hon. member, I am confident that we are expressing the views of thousands of good, solid, patriotic Canadians. I say this because I have had the opportunity of having conversations with supporters of all parties in this house. I have received letters from the supporters of all parties in this house, which indicate that there are large numbers of Canadians who are opposed to this measure because they are sincerely opposed to German rearmament.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare when speaking this afternoon suggested to the house that there might even be enthusiasm in the country for this measure. I think the tenor of this debate has indicated

there is no enthusiasm for this measure, because almost every member has expressed his justifiable fears of German rearmament and the possibilities of the future. I know that the communists in Canada are opposed to German rearmament. I know of the campaign they have waged in the country and even in this building. In my opinion that is no reason for my views to be affected.
This afternoon the Minister of National Health and Welfare read into the record a directive issued by the labour progressive party to its members. As the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) suggested he made, I think, a rather unfortunate inference, though he later qualified that statement. I much prefer the attitude of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) when you come to consider a situation of this nature.
In British Columbia the Liberals, the supporters of the C.C.F. and the labour progressives have expressed opposition to the building of what is known as the Kaiser dam on the lower Arrow lakes. I am informed that the labour progressive party has advised its members to campaign against the building of that dam. This fact does not influence my opinion one bit. I was glad to notice that, according to newspaper reports, it does not influence the opinion of the Minister of Fisheries. In a speech in British Columbia he mentioned that the Liberals, many C.C.F., communists and others opposed the building of the Kaiser dam, but the minister was apparently quite willing to let the issue be settled and dealt with on its merits. We take exactly the same view in a situation such as this.
I fully appreciate the difficulties, doubts and fears which this problem presents to the members of this house. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that along with other members in this group I most sincerely respect the views of those who disagree with us.
My opposition to this resolution is based mainly on two grounds. Personally, I fear the rearmament of Germany. In presenting my case I shall try to deal with the matter on a logical basis, although I am one who has had some experience with unconventional methods of warfare on the part of German militarism.
I oppose this resolution in the second place because I believe, in common with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that this step will increase the danger of war. I believe it is an irrevocable step in further widening the division between the east and the west.

The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell)-and I listened to his remarks attentively-said he could not understand why those who voted for NATO cannot vote for this measure, or words to that effect. Mr. Speaker, because one votes for the establishment of a committee on procedure it does not necessarily mean that he is going to vote for all the things that committee does. Consequently I suggest that this is a somewhat different matter from voting in support of NATO, or in support of bringing into NATO recognized western democratic nations.
I think the hon. member for Greenwood said he could not understand why we are opposed to German rearmament and increased strength. In the opinion of those who are opposing the measure we believe the military advantages do not equal the risk. We are of the opinion that if you increase the German military forces by 12 divisions, or whatever the stated number may be, you are simply causing the Soviet bloc on the other side to increase their forces to a similar extent and that therefore, in the long run, you accomplish nothing so far as increased defence is concerned.
The hon. member for Greenwood also suggested that he could not understand our opposing increased armaments, or having our military strength increased; but we
North Atlantic Treaty
believe at the present time we are not negotiating from weakness but rather that we are already negotiating from strength.
My reading of published documents, newspapers, magazines and periodicals, and my study of this whole situation brings me definitely to certain conclusions. And as I have reached a point where I shall have to proceed with my argument, perhaps owing to the time I should now move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. Herridge the debate was adjourned.
